#3721. Nintendo tried adding fast travel to The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, before devs realised "we were missing out on the moments of discovery"

"I thought we needed to address this in this new version."

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is being wrapped up in all kinds of modern touches for its imminent Nintendo Switch 2 remake (that owl seems to be less chatty, for starters), but there's at least one quality-of-life feature borrowed from Breath of the Wild that the developers felt was better left on the cutting room floor: fast travel.

In Nintendo's latest Ask The Developer blog post, long-time series producer Eiji Aonuma explained that he initially asked the game's remakers to add warp points so players could get around Hyrule without having to spam rolls and presumably make Link violently ill in the process. But he and the team quickly realised fast travel doesn't work so well in a game that's still, in its bones, almost three decades old.

"In The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild, there are many warp points that enable players to move quickly around the game's vast world. In the original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, you could get around a bit faster by spamming forward roll, so I think a lot of players spent their time doggedly rolling across Hyrule Field whenever they needed to be somewhere in a hurry," Aonuma said.

"I thought we needed to address this in this new version. So I asked the team to add warp points that didn't exist in the original game, giving players access to shortcuts. But when we actually tried playing the game with those warp points, we realized that we were missing out on the moments of discovery that came from stopping along the way and wondering, 'Wait, what's this?' Through this development process, we were reminded once again just how important those moments are to the very structure of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. So even though I was the one who proposed adding warp points, they just weren't working for me in the end, so I got the team to take them all back out again."

There you have it. No fast-travel points in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's remake, and it sounds like it's for the best. I avoided warping around Breath of the Wild's open world for the same reasons Aonuma laid out - spotting something odd way in the distance, slowly finding a way to reach it, and then discovering a funky little Korok seed was always a thrill that wouldn't have been possible by cutting out the trek in between main objectives.

Talking about why Nintendo chose to revive Ocarina of Time now, Aonuma said some of the younger developers on the team had maybe never played the original game 28 years ago, and remaking it could "trigger new insights that they can carry forward into future development."

As for the remake's somewhat divisive art style, art director Aya Shida said the team "used phrases like 'a puppet-show feel' and 'the analog feel of practical effects films'" early on in production. "Neither puppet shows nor practical effects films reproduce reality exactly as it is. Even so, both create a convincing sense that the characters truly exist within their respective fantasy worlds," Shida continued.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time comes out on the 5th of November. After getting some hands-on time with the revival, Lottie thought it was shaping up to be a brilliant remake.

#3720. Little Shop of Horrors: An Oral History

Like an unassuming plant from outer space, Little Shop of Horrors had humble beginnings—but managed to blossom at a surprising rate. The musical is performed numerous times each year across the globe; the current Off Broadway production has been running for seven years straight. But none of that would have happened without the 1986 film version of Little Shop, a cult classic that Warner Bros. executives once characterized as “the highest-budget musical they’d ever done,” according to its director, Frank Oz. “I don’t know if it’s true or if it’s hyperbole, but that’s what they told me to pressure me into doing a good job.”

“I love it. Audiences love it,” says composer Alan Menken. “Anytime I watch Little Shop,” though, “every other second I’ll be thinking about my late collaborator”—lyricist, book writer, and original stage director Howard Ashman, whom he worked with on both the original stage show and the film. “I’ll look at his work and how amazing it is,” Menken says. “Then people come running up to me, and I go, ‘It’s Howard.’”

Moranis as Seymour Krelborn and Ellen Greene as Audrey in Frank Oz's 1986 film adaptation.

It’s been nearly 40 years since Audrey II began its cinematic rampage. To commemorate the movie—which is getting a brand-new 4K restoration and rerelease on Blu-ray—Vanity Fair spoke with Oz, Menken, producer David Geffen, stars Rick Moranis, Ellen Greene, Tisha Campbell, Tichina Arnold, Michelle Weeks, and more about assembling an A-list cast including Steve Martin and Bill Murray; the film’s long, difficult production; why Moranis had to film several of his scenes as though he was moving in slow motion; and the movie’s elaborate, expensive, utterly depressing original ending.

Back in 1959, legendary low-budget filmmaker Roger Corman had a challenge: to shoot an entire film in two days. He enlisted Charles B. Griffith to write a film using preexisting sets—including a florist shop and a dental office. The original Little Shop of Horrors was born: a scrappy but ambitious B movie featuring a brief cameo by a young Jack Nicholson.

The film became a staple of late-night television, entrancing viewers like a teenage Howard Ashman. As an adult, Ashman knew it’d make a great musical. His agent watched the Corman film and told Ashman he was out of his mind.

Poster for the TV adaptation of The Little Shop of Horrors, 1960.

Ashman then approached jingle writer Alan Menken about doing the musical with him at the WPA Theatre, of which Ashman was a cofounder.

ALAN MENKEN (COMPOSER): I thought it was absolutely amazing. This was one of those so-bad-it’s-good movies. When we first took a crack [at writing the songs], it was actually very close to the Corman film…. And then Howard said, “You know, I think we should do this as the dark side of Grease.”

You think about those beach blanket horror movies from the early ’60s or late ’50s, and there is both a tackiness and an incredible exuberance about them at the same time. And then you think about the Phil Spector Wall of Sound and his work with the Ronettes. So the score became a whole homage to all those early rock influences, and it just became a perfect tonal bed for the storytelling.

ELLEN GREENE (“AUDREY,” ORIGINAL OFF BROADWAY AND THE 1986 FILM): I got to watch Howard direct several sessions with Alan playing on the piano. They counterbalanced each other; Howard was very serious, and Alan is just a sweetheart. Although Howard was also a sweetheart.

MENKEN: What makes for a good collaboration, first of all, is to get your fucking egos out of the room. Bring your talent into the room and always be ready to throw something out…. Don’t ever allow yourself to fall in love with your own work. You are driving this particular thing called a musical. Howard was the best I ever experienced at doing that…. Howard knew exactly what he wanted.

GREENE: I remember walking down the street [listening to a demo of the song “Skid Row” and thinking], I don’t want to do a camp musical. [Then I] got too unemployed, and I'm listening to “Somewhere That’s Green.” I started quietly singing “Green” to myself, and it made me cry. And I knew right then and there I had an Audrey inside of me that was waiting to be born…. When I went into the audition, I did the scenes, and the speaking voice just came out of me.

Michelle Weeks, Tisha Campbell, and Tichina Arnold as Chiffon, Crystal, and Ronette, respectively, in the 1986 adaptation.

LEE WILKOF (“SEYMOUR,” ORIGINAL OFF BROADWAY): I got a call from a casting director that I knew in New York. [She said], “A theater in New York is doing a musical based on the movie Little Shop of Horrors…. Would you come in and read for the part of the dentist? I walked into the audition…and Howard Ashman looked at me and he went, “You’re not a dentist. Would you mind going out and looking at the role of Seymour?” And I did, and I got a callback. Apparently, it was between me and another actor. His name’s Nathan Lane. And the assistant director apparently said that she thought that I would work better as a Seymour. Her name’s Connie Grappo, and we’ve been married 42 years.

GREENE: I was a brunette at the time. I said, “Howie, meet me at 14th Street.”… And I tried on a long blonde wig with bangs, and he went, “I don’t know what you’re doing.” I said, “Just let me finish.” Paul Holmes, the stage manager, helped me cut the wig, and Howard still wasn’t sure. Then I completed the look [with a black cocktail dress], and he loved it.

The show opened at the WPA in 1982 for what was supposed to be a two-week “showcase,” with the actors all making a mere $50 a week in exchange for being reviewed by major theater critics. It was an immediate success.

WILKOF: It was impossible to get a ticket. It went from being this obscure little show. The word on the street apparently grew.

MENKEN: We had lines of producers around the block.

DAVID GEFFEN (PRODUCER): I don’t quite remember how I first got involved, but I think Cameron Mackintosh and I were approached…. I thought it was terrific.

Director of photography Robert Paynter on set, 1986.

MENKEN: We knew there were people who wanted to bring Little Shop to Broadway, and Howard said absolutely not.

GEFFEN: The [Off Broadway] show was very successful, highly thought of. Then we opened it up in Los Angeles. It was natural that we’d make it as a movie.

The creative team began planning a feature film, which Geffen would produce. Tom Cruise, per Menken, wanted to play Seymour (although his reps have claimed he wasn’t interested in the role); he was immediately vetoed by Ashman. Geffen had his eyes set instead on a comedic actor from Canada.

RICK MORANIS (“SEYMOUR”): I first started hearing about the film being made early on, like ’82 or ’83. I ran into David Geffen randomly—I had never met him before—and he stopped me and said, “I want you in my movie.” I said, “Which one?” And he told me, and I said, “Well, okay!” And then for the next three years, I would occasionally hear about it or read about it in the hands of one director or another, and nothing ever happened.

At one point, Steven Spielberg was slated to produce the film, with Martin Scorsese directing. John Landis was also attached to the project for a time. Perhaps the name that made the most sense on paper was Frank Oz, best known as the man who brought to life childhood staples like Miss Piggy, Fozzie Bear, and Yoda.

FRANK OZ (DIRECTOR): I saw [the show] and thought it was amazing. But I didn’t have a take on it. And when I read the script for the movie, I couldn’t get my hands around it. It was so big, and I didn’t have a clear vision of it. So, through my agents, I said, “Thank you, but I can’t do it.” Two weeks later, something clicked in me regarding the three girl-group singers. I realized that when they entered onstage, all they could do was enter from the left or from the right…. But in a movie, it’s 360 degrees; you can have them enter from anywhere. So that’s what kind of changed my idea. I called back and I said, “You know, I may have a way to do this,” and then David asked me to do a rewrite…. Then I went to London, and I spent a month on the rewrite, and I felt really good about it. I knew if I said yes [to directing it], that’d mean two years of my life would be on this project. But I was committed and excited about it.

GREENE: [Frank] has to see the vision. Until he sees the vision in his mind’s eye, in his head, he will not take something on.

Greene, Steve Martin as Orin Scrivello, and Moranis, 1986.

MORANIS: [It’s] the intersection of so many skills and qualities that he has: a remarkable sense of humor, a real affinity for the darker arts and all the puppeteering, and such a keen eye for design.

OZ: I had not known Rick, who is now one of my closest friends after all these years. I never knew Rick, never heard of him because I was in London shooting for five years, and Rick was doing SCTV, and that was not shown in London. But I saw some of his work and I thought it was brilliant.

MORANIS: I knew this was an extraordinary opportunity to do a musical, and shoot it in London, and work with Frank and that cast. [Film] musicals don’t come along too often for people who get to call themselves actors.

OZ: David understandably wanted a star, but…I couldn’t see an Audrey with the depth and the heart that was given to the character by Ellen. I couldn’t see that being done by anyone else. So I asked him to please let me do a screen test with Ellen, and he did. And that’s when David said yes to Ellen.

MORANIS: Ellen had created the character of Audrey for the Off Broadway show many years before we did the movie.  She wasn’t just acting the part of Audrey; she was Audrey. I had just come from years of comedic character acting on SCTV and in films like Strange Brew and Ghostbusters. So we were both approaching our performances for Little Shop in similar ways. I think that’s why we had such a strong onscreen chemistry.

GREENE: Frank saw the character a little more heroine-like [than she was onstage]. He wasn’t sure about the “Audrey-isms,” and so that’s why the line “You don’t meet nice boys when you live on Skid Row, Mr. Mushnik” is not in the film…. Freddy Cooper was a cameraman…and he’s the reason I got to do the squeak in the film. Frank and Rick weren’t sure, and he spoke up and said, “Sir, I think it’s funny.”

OZ: David also suggested Steve Martin, and Steve I had worked with a little bit prior to that. Steve and I talked, and at the time there was a very popular character called Fonzie, and Steve said he just didn’t want to do Fonzie. I said, “Absolutely, that’s fine.” He wanted it more like Elvis. I said, “Fantastic.” As far as I was concerned, Steve could do anything.

The film’s glue wasn’t any of its big names; it was the three girls, all under 18, who made up its ’60s-girl-group-esque Greek chorus.

TISHA CAMPBELL (“CHIFFON”): I had just auditioned to play Regina King’s best friend in 227, and I didn’t get it. So I quit. I was 16 years old. I wanted to go to camp with my friends. And while I was there, my mother called me. She said, “Your agent keeps bugging me. They won’t stop calling me.” I said, “Did you tell them I quit?” And she said, “I told them and said you just wanted to be a regular kid, and they were like, ‘Please, just this one audition. Then you can go to camp.’ Can you just do it and I’ll send you right back to camp? No harm, no foul.” And I was like, “Okay, fine.”

MICHELLE WEEKS (“RONETTE”): At the time, I was on Broadway doing Tap Dance Kid, and I had a management company submit me. When I went for the audition…I was like, Yeah, they’re not gonna pick me. I’m too big. But then when we went for the callbacks, I was like, Oh, I have a chance!

Steve Ross, Courtney Sale, Steven Spielberg, and David Geffen at an off-Broadway performance of Little Shop of Horrors, 1982.

TICHINA ARNOLD (“CRYSTAL”): [I was] starting off in the theater [as] a little kid with wide eyes and ready to get it cracking. I just so happened to know Michelle Weeks because she and I went to school together. We had the same friends, and then Tisha and I knew each other from just auditioning.

CAMPBELL: They auditioned girls from everywhere…. And it just so happened that [the three girls cast were] from the tristate area. Michelle was from Brooklyn, Tichina was from Queens, and I was from New Jersey.

ARNOLD: And Frank Oz, we asked him, “How did you choose us?” And he was just like, “You girls had a synergy.”

Little Shop presented a real technical challenge: how to capture chemistry between its lead, Rick Moranis, and the man-eating plant. For the voice of the plant—named Audrey II by Seymour—the creative team turned to Motown singer Levi Stubbs. But actually bringing the creature to life would be the real struggle.

OZ: There’s only two words necessary, and that’s [puppeteer] Lyle Conway. Lyle passed recently, sadly, but Lyle is the one responsible for the plant. He was a pure artist, and he did an incredible job.

BRIAN HENSON (PRINCIPAL PUPPETEER): I think [Lyle] brought almost everybody that was on Return to Oz, and then a lot more because it was a much bigger build…. My dad [Jim Henson] came and visited the shoot a couple times, for sure. And then my little sister, Heather, was in it. She’s in the dentist scene.

BRAN FERREN (SPECIAL VISUAL EFFECTS): Lyle Conway was brilliant, his vision for how to create—because there wasn’t one plant; there were a series of plants that were used to show its various stages of growth.

OZ: I needed pure lip sync, really good lip sync, not just a mouth opening and closing. Because you’re on film, they can see in a tight shot that it’s just a puppet if it’s just opening and closing.

HENSON: This was definitely the biggest and the most complex [thing] that had ever been done in animatronics. It was also before the Creature Shop–type people were using motors, so it was almost all cable-driven.

OZ: All the performers had to rehearse the song over and over and over to make sure they hit every single syllable.

HENSON: There’s no eyes on that character, so it was always going to be the physical presence of the plant combined with this mouth and this voice. So Levi’s recordings were very important to Frank. [But] we started rehearsing before he even had Levi’s recordings.

MORANIS: They were looking for ways to make vowels and consonants so that they could form words, and then form phrases, and then be able to do that to music. And it was only possible to do at a slower motion than 24 frames a second.

There are 24 still frames in every second of standard film. But during rehearsals, it was discovered that the plant could not believably lip-synch at that speed. The production’s solution was to slow down Audrey II’s motions—operating the plant at 12 frames per second, then speeding the film up later so that it would look normal. This meant that anytime Moranis was in the same shot as the plant, he also had to move, act, and sing in slow motion.

MORANIS: The trick was to keep my butt tight. Because we keep our butt tight when we’re walking quickly. And when you try and walk slowly, it’s very easy to let your butt relax. If you were to look at that at 24 frames, you would look like you were doing some sort of weird walk. So by keeping the butt tight, I managed to pull it off, I think.

GREENE: [Frank] taught me how to act at 12 frames per second. He put me in a room; he had a camera. He said, “Ellen, walk across the floor.” He set it up to the regular speed. He said, “Now look at this,” and it looked like I was rocking back and forth. He showed me how you have to walk only forward, and ballet sort of helped. I worked on acting, talking, and moving in 12 frames a second.

John Candy as Wink Wilkinson and Moranis as Seymour Krelborn, 1986.

FERREN: How do you put emotion into a plant? I mean, news flash: It wasn’t a real man-eating plant! And my suspicion is that not many people watching the movie said, “Oh my God, they found an actual man-eating plant.” If you get it right, they shouldn’t be thinking about that.

HENSON: When we started rehearsing, we just had a bit of skin for the lips. The head was bald, and it was quite lightweight. Every week they’d build a little bit more, and it would just get heavier and heavier and heavier. By the end, it weighed more than 150 pounds.

With the cast—and plant—in place, filming began on October 21, 1985, at Pinewood Studios on the 007 Stage. Per Frank Oz’s vision, it had to be done entirely on a soundstage, as the world they were creating couldn’t come to life on location.

OZ: Roy Walker, our brilliant production designer, and I walked through the whole set. I told him where I felt things needed to be for each particular number, because I had planned the numbers in my head months before I even got to London.

GREENE: [As] someone who first was on this tiny, tiny stage, [I walked] into Pinewood Studios…and there in front of me is the land that is built, that I only saw in my mind's eye because I was on the stage—and it’s even better than I ever imagined.

OZ: My goal was to make it a movie sensibility instead of only a theatrical sensibility. It’s really a mixture of it, and my real goal was to make sure it reflected the gritty atmosphere of an Off Broadway play, and not a musical. I didn’t want to make it into Hello, Dolly! or Mame.

MENKEN: Little Shop is meant to be this tacky show in a hole-in-the-wall…and they wanted the film to have that same quality.

OZ: The opening number is packed with information. You have the three girls dancing in the streets. I needed people to know that they were not regular human beings, so I had them sing in the rain—and they were not affected by the rain.

ARNOLD: Frank Oz explained to us, “It’s gonna be raining around you, but you won’t get wet.” And I was like, “How is that gonna happen?” He showed us the pipes and stuff that they had in the ceiling and said, “Okay, so choreography-wise, you’re gonna follow this path [to ensure you don’t get wet].”

CAMPBELL: Man, it was raining on our heads! The first time we filmed that scene, it was raining so hard that you could tell on our faces. They had to cut. They were like, “You can’t show that it’s raining on y’all!”

WEEKS: We had to be up early in the morning, and us being teenagers, we were going places we weren’t supposed to go, like the club. We used to go to the Hippodrome and get out at like two or three in the morning, and have to be at the studio at six. But it was so much fun!

OZ: I loved shooting “Suddenly Seymour.” When Roy showed me the set—which is beautiful—I saw that staircase that he made. I thought, Okay, it’s got to be a Romeo-and-Juliet section where she’s up there, and he’s down there, and he runs up there. So it was all built up to that moment. I had him run up the stairs 30 to 40 times.

GREENE: Fifty-three takes we had to go up those stairs. [The “Suddenly Seymour”] set was so beautiful, with grass growing through the cracks and bricks and cobblestones. If any set was ever called a work of art, I think this would be applicable.

CAMPBELL: [Steve Martin] was very quiet off camera. But when that camera rolled, I was just in awe of how he would light up and become this character, and just be very big and broad.

OZ: When David suggested Billy [Murray, who has a cameo in the dentist scene]—and I knew Billy before that—I called him. I said, “Hey, Billy, do you want to do this?” And Bill said, “Do I have to do the words?” And I said, “No. I don’t care what words you use as long as you’re the masochist and he’s the sadist. That’s all I care about.”

As technical as the film itself was, nothing could compare to the plant.

OZ: People tend to think, Oh, puppets, that’s no problem. They are the hardest things in the world to shoot, to do right…. Just “Feed Me” alone took five weeks to shoot.

HENSON: Nowadays, you think of a film unit shooting 30 to 40 setups a day. Little Shop of Horrors was way down at three to five, five to seven if you were shooting easier stuff. It was slow, meticulous shooting. And Frank is a very meticulous director.

OZ: We’d usually go about 25 to 30 takes to make it perfect.

MORANIS: [For] “Feed Me,” Brian was inside the head of the plant, and then all the other puppeteers were connected to the plant. The actual plant store that we shot in was constructed on the second floor, and the first floor is where the puppeteers set up camp and where their cables would go down to. They would have monitors, and they could watch themselves operate the plant.

HENSON: There were vines that were being worked by one or two people on each vine. It [took] maybe five of us to work the head…. With “Mean Green Mother”…there’d be puppeteers all the way around the outside of the set, doing cables, and on the roof of the set was another maybe 10 puppeteers. And the set was also on top of a tank, so they could get to the underside of the pot for the roots.

MORANIS: It was so enjoyable to do [“Feed Me”]. I don’t think I had a moment when I didn’t enjoy shooting it. I do remember one aspect, just because it went on for so long: Every day I would come in and put on the same clothes.[Just] put on the same clothes every day for five weeks, or whatever it was.

HENSON: [During “Feed Me”], I’m right there. I said to Lyle, “You know, I just can’t stay hidden all the time.”… I couldn’t hide completely behind the stem. And Lyle said, “Okay, this is what we’re going to do. You’re going to wear a skintight green Lycra suit, and I’m gonna glue leaves to it.” There’s bits of me in the shots, but you don’t know it’s me.

The stage version of Little Shop ends with the plant eating Audrey, Seymour, and, finally, the audience. The filmmakers were determined to capture that same spirit, and did so in a $5 million epic ending that saw Audrey II taking over New York—ending on top of the Statue of Liberty.

OZ: Before I even went to London, I was at David Geffen’s office, and David said to us, “You know, you can’t end it the way the play ends it, because you’re killing your leads.” And Howard and I both said, “Well, we want to be true to the ending from Off Broadway, in part because we just like being true to things, but also because it was a deal with the devil. He deserved to die because he killed people, even though he didn’t do it maliciously.”

GREENE: I gravitate to the dark underpinnings of the Faustian tale. Even though there's a magical world full of whimsy and silliness and goofiness, it has a moral with dark underpinnings.

OZ: Richard Conway had worked about nine months on the models of the destruction at the end. It was no CGI, no opticals. Richard had built all this stuff, and then built the small plant that would be on the bridge, and he did an incredible job having the plants like Godzilla raging through the city.

MORANIS: I remember that, when I saw the ending of the play, something was off with it, but it didn’t matter because the vines came out of the ceiling. And I thought, This is brilliant! They’re distracting you from the tragic ending by creating this fun experience of stuff flying out of the ceiling.You’re part of the action. The shock and surprise, and all the tactile fuzziness of it, distracted from whatever was lacking in a fulfilling happy ending. It didn’t occur to me that that would become a problem in the film.

This is Audrey II in Little Shop of Horrors, 1986.

GREENE: In the play, I say a line—“When I die, which should be very shortly…”—just to lighten the moment, and it’s silly. It releases some of the energy in the audience. But when I say it in the film, it’s very intimate, and it’s to Seymour. It’s weighted differently…. I’m very proud of that scene.

MENKEN: When we did [the first] preview…I'm sitting there going, “Wow! Look at this!” I look at David Geffen, and he said, “Yeah, wow, but wait a second—the cards, Alan!”

Those would be the reaction cards on which that era’s preview audiences would answer questions regarding how much they liked a film. Typically, producers were looking for 55% of a screening’s viewers to say they’d “recommend” the film. Little Shop’s first screening in San Jose got 13%. Oz asked Geffen to screen it again in LA to make sure this wasn’t an anomaly. The results were the same.

GEFFEN: People were hostile to the end of the film. They were hostile to the characters getting killed. We thought we were going to have a disaster.

OZ: The audience was against me because I killed people they loved, and it was a great lesson to learn. Onstage, they also die, but the actors come out for a bow. In movies, you don’t come out for a bow. You just die.

GREENE: [Onstage], my death is not as heartbreaking. It's a mixture. Just when you’re about to laugh, I’ll make you cry. Just when you’re about to cry, I’ll make you laugh.

GEFFEN: I think what the audience didn’t get was that this was a send-up of monster movies in the ’50s. They took it quite seriously. We made it so realistic that they were horrified by the end of the movie.

FERREN: The idea was, I want to go out smiling and happy. Now, I guess, it shows my personality. I went out smiling and happy, watching the world end.

OZ: They wouldn’t even release the movie if I didn’t change the ending…. The hardest of all was the terrible, terrible, terrible phone call I had to make after Richard Conway and his amazing crew made all those miniatures in that whole ending. I remember I had to call London from Los Angeles and say, “Richard, we’re not going to use any of it.”

What I also heard at the time [after the failed test screenings] was that there was a thought to try and get Rodney Dangerfield to do the voice of the plant, I assume to make it funny. My intent for the plant was to have it [be] a strong antagonist. If it was funny, there would have been no threat to Seymour or Audrey.

The team had to figure out a new finale that would stay true to the story and give Seymour and Audrey a happy ending. The solution? Seymour would electrocute the plant during their final showdown, and he and Audrey would finally get to move somewhere that’s green. But sitting outside of their dream home would be a small Audrey II, smiling at the camera.

OZ: The idea [came together] very fast. Howard and I knew exactly what had to happen. That part where the little plant smiles at the end was because I couldn’t make it a happy ending. It had to have some danger to it…. We went back [to London] for a month to reshoot.

Made on a budget of $25 million, including $5 million that wound up on the cutting-room floor, the film was unleashed on the public on December 19, 1986. It wound up doubling its budget at the box office, earning $54 million globally. A modest success, it didn’t necessarily set the world on fire—at least, not right away.

ARNOLD: Tisha and I had a really interesting moment. We decided to go see the movie in Times Square. We sat behind these two girls that were watching it, and we were like, “Okay, let’s go in when it’s dark so nobody recognizes us.”

CAMPBELL: There were these three girls sitting behind us. And [during the movie], they were like, “I’m so sick of these girls popping up out of nowhere!” [Laughs] So our first experience being able to watch our film, there were some haters behind us.

ARNOLD: Needless to say, I don’t watch myself anymore.

MENKEN: “Mean Green Mother” was nominated for the Academy Award, which was just amazing. I remember Levi Stubbs came out and sang “Mean Green Mother.” And I'm thinking, Wow! Well, I have a speech in my pocket. Who knows? Howard just goes, “Alan, you can relax. You’re not giving any speeches tonight.”

OZ: [When it came to home video], that’s when everything kind of exploded.

GREENE: [While currently touring with the movie], I get to see their love of Little Shop, their love of Audrey, even their love of me. I just hug everybody because I know they want it.

WEEKS: I went to see [Ellen on the tour recently]. It brought me to tears a couple of times…. They introduced me, and Ellen was surprised to see me. I was so happy to see her. We hugged and everything, and we talked a bit later on. But the warm reception that I got kind of brought me to tears because they were like, “Oh my gosh, it’s Ronette!” It just made me feel seen.

ARNOLD: I always said Little Shop of Horrors was a movie done before its time. But it stood the test of time and is still standing.

MENKEN: It is a true musical, and it’s driven by high-energy pop and rock, and it’s not about, “Oh, look how hip it is.”… It’s a thrill ride that really moves fast.

GEFFEN: I thought it was a terrific movie when we made it. I was very unhappy that we changed the ending…. I always wanted to restore it. And, as you know, we did. [In 2017 a version of the movie with the original ending played in theaters.]

OZ: I finally got to call Richard before he retired, saying, “Richard, finally they’re going to see your work.”

MORANIS: It’s become a point of discussion for people, whether they prefer one to the other, or if they’ve seen both of them. It’s prompted a couple of extra releases of different versions of the film.

OZ: I think [it resonates] because when you look at the movie, you know it’s not CGI…. It’s nice to show people what could be done when a lot of human beings get together and make something.

#3719. The Borderlands series has sold over 100 million copies, and Gearbox is "cooking hard on more Borderlands 4 content for next year"

The Borderlands series has sold more than 100m copies across all games, developer Gearbox Software has announced. No surprise, then - the studio also said it's cooking up "big plans" for the evergreen looter shooter's future.

"The Borderlands franchise has officially crossed 100 million units sold," Gearbox boasted in a blog post published today. "There aren't many franchises that have ever hit that milestone, and we certainly didn't get here on our own. For us, it started with that first Borderlands in 2009, and we've been excited about everyone who has joined us in the Borderlands along the way. Borderlands has always had an incredibly passionate community. We've been through a lot together, and your feedback pushes us to make even greater games."

So, where can Vault Hunters expect to go next? Gearbox just finished up on Borderlands 4's Year One roadmap - which included two new playable characters, two Story Packs and more - and it's now "cooking hard on more Borderlands 4 content for next year." There's no concrete information about what that looks like for now, but the studio promised Weekly Activity refreshes and Community Challenges will chug on in the meantime.

"We're also taking a bigger look at the franchise as a whole. Where can we take it next? What characters do you want to spend more time with? What stories deserve a payoff? A huge part of that is listening to you," the studio wrote. "All that said, big plans take time, and we need some room to work. You can trust that we'll talk more when the time is right. Now is your chance to influence what we'll say."

Borderlands 4 itself experienced a "softer" than expected launch, thanks partly to the game's wonky PC performance, though it seems to have been a success in the long run. A promised Switch 2 port was also indefinitely delayed earlier in the year. We haven't heard much about that handheld version since, but Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick did say the team were focusing on getting Borderlands 4 into tip-top shape before trying to bring it elsewhere.

In Eurogamer's Borderlands 4 review, Rick Lane said the shooter bought a "more sensible script and a true open world to its pseudo-cel-shaded gun-show, but these moderate improvements are undermined by frustrating exploration and combat that takes too long to properly shine."

#3718. GTA 6 Pre-Load Times, Install Size, And Global Release Times Confirmed

Grand Theft Auto 6Grand Theft Auto VIGTA 6Pre-Load

We’re just over two weeks out from the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6 and Rockstar Games has finally revealed all of the details people need to know about getting the digital-only open-world game installed on their gaming console of choice.

The studio also confirmed that, yes, GTA 6 has a whopping 212GB install size, so start making room for that and god help you if you have an Xbox Series S. Here’s everything you need to know about getting GTA 6 ready to play for its release on November 19, 2026.

Digital pre-loading on PlayStation 5 will start globally on Tuesday, November 10 at midnight local time. On Xbox Series X|S, pre-loading begins globally on Tuesday, November 10 at 12 a.m. GMT, which is 7:00 p.m. ET on the previous day, November 9.

If you pre-order GTA 6 digitally, you’ll have access to pre-load the game immediately. If you are waiting for one of the codes in a box to ship to your home or be picked up in store, those will become available starting November 12. You’ll be able to take that code, redeem it, and immediately start pre-loading the game.

That’s a big file size, and console servers are going to get hammered when everyone starts trying to download it at once. To put it in perspective, 212GB is roughly one third of the available storage on a base PS5 and roughly a quarter of the available storage on a 1TB model. On Xbox Series S, it’s closer to half. In addition to taking some time depending on the speed of your internet, you’ll want to make sure you have your library cleared of any non-essential games. Good luck to you if you have children who are constantly swapping between a dozen different games every day.

The global release times for when GTA 6 goes live were previously announced, and unfortunately the U.S. is one of the last time zones to get access to the game.

Yes, the game will have been out in some parts of the world for roughly 18 hours by the time GTA 6 goes live stateside. My advice is to just stay logged out that day.

This week, Bethesda Game Studios is celebrating its 40th birthday—a celebration that included the full name reveal of The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel, successfully completing the eight-year task of adding a word to a thing.

In addition, Bethesda is commemorating the occasion with the launch of a 40th anniversary site collecting the anecdotes and favorite memories of studio staff, including one Alan Nanes. Now a design director, Nanes was originally hired at Bethesda as one of its first full-time QA testers—and by his own description, he got the job by being a pleasant fellow to spend time with.

According to Nanes, his history with Bethesda started during Morrowind's development. He was close friends with Bethesda devs in multiple departments, and it was an era where that was enough to get you in the building.

"Things were a bit 'Wild West' back then, and my friends allowed me to hang out (yes, before I was an employee) there, playing multiplayer games with them and just getting to know everyone," Nanes wrote. "Eventually, Todd Howard noticed my presence in the studio and asked if I wanted to test out their new game."

In time, his impromptu testing sessions started attracting an audience of Bethesda developers who would pick his brain about their design choices, scribble notes, and debate with each other about potential tweaks to the game while watching over his shoulder.

"It was an extraordinary feeling, the first time I felt like I was contributing to the creation of an actual videogame (I believe you can find my name in the Morrowind manual's credits under 'Special Thanks')," Nanes said. "After this became a regular occurrence, Todd Howard and Ashley Cheng seemed to decide having full-time, in-studio QA would be a valuable addition to the team, and I took on that mantle."

Nanes later graduated to a quest designer position for Oblivion, and was more recently credited as lead companions designer on Starfield. But while his tenure at Bethesda might've had a storybook trajectory, the history of QA workers at the studio has been a contentious one in the years since Nanes was hired.

From the creators of Edge: A free weekly videogame industry newsletter, featuring in-depth news, expert analysis and exclusive interviews

Driven by frustrations surrounding compensation, advancement opportunities, workload, and more, QA workers at Bethesda's parent company ZeniMax initiated a unionization vote in 2022, officially forming ZeniMax Workers United - CWA—then the largest videogame union in the US—when the vote succeeded in January 2023.

Those frustrations remained unaddressed as contract negotiations with Microsoft stalled for over two years, driving the QA union to vote overwhelmingly in favor of authorizing a strike in April 2025. Its contract was ultimately ratified in June 2025. When a number of those QA workers were affected by Xbox's July 2026 layoffs, that contract allowed the union to enter into an "effects bargaining" process to negotiate severance terms for its impacted members, culminating in "a significant agreement" in September 2026.

#3716. Yakuza creator's new studio and its debut game Gang of Dragon are no more after losing funding from NetEase

Nagoshi Studio has officially shut down and its first game called Gang of Dragon is seemingly no more, months after publisher NetEase pulled funding from the Yakuza-like project.

Toshihiro Nagoshi (often cited as the creator of the brilliant Yakuza and Like A Dragon game series) opened his new studio in 2021 and announced his next game with a very familiar title almost one year ago. Now, the Tokyo-based developer has closed its doors, as confirmed in the Japanese government gazette Kanpo.

The news comes months after employees were told that the studio's future was at risk due to NetEase's funding cuts. Nagoshi Studio reportedly needed another £33.1 million (about $44.4m at the time) to get Gang of Dragon past the finish line - a paycheck NetEase purportedly didn't want to cough up.

The China-based Marvel Rivals and Where Winds Meet publisher has been significantly scaling back on international investments these past few years. Visions of Mana developer Ouka Studios was shut down just after launching its gorgeous action game, Worlds Untold (a studio formed by Mass Effect veteran Mac Walters) had to pause operations to find a new partner, and Halo Infinite lead Jerry Hook's studio also ran into very similar issues last year.

Some developers have been a little luckier. Suda51's Grasshopper Manufacture saved itself with a management buyout and now operates as an independent developer, for one.

Not much is known about Gang of Dragon, but its debut trailer featured the violent crime and high drama you'd expect from Nagoshi's previous work. The game also starred Ma Dong-seok, the acclaimed actor you might recognise from films such as Train to Busan and Marvel's Eternals.

Parks and Recreation has been off the air for over ten years, but I still find myself coming back to the workplace sitcom whenever I need to improve my mood. Pawnee feels like home; the characters always make me laugh, the heartwarming moments always make me cry, and I feel like I walk away from every rewatch having been taught a new life lesson.

Tom and Donna’s “Treat yo self” mantra, Leslie’s endless optimism, and Ron’s quiet way of loving and supporting those around him are just a few of the life lessons I’ve learned as a fan. As fans, we’re always more susceptible to latching on to characters and learning lessons because of how many times we’ll rewatch something; but stars themselves can also learn something from their time on a show. Case in point: Amy Poehler recently opened up about what playing one of the most beloved television characters of all time taught her.

Leslie Knope taught me a lot. Playing her really did improve my life. It made me a much better listener and more engaged person in the world. And it was really nice to come to work and, like, spend the whole day telling everybody how much you love them. I had to have a lot of energy to play her. And she gave me a lot of energy when I played her.

Parks and Rec was full of hilarious characters with big hearts, but it was Leslie who centered them all. Sure, sometimes she tried too hard and failed, but she always did things because she thought it would make a difference for the people of Pawnee. She’s definitely the reason why I always come back to the show and consider it one of the best sitcoms of all time.

To me, Poehler and Knope are basically the same person. Anyone who has ever listened to the Saturday Night Live alum speak over the years can attest to the way she seems to embody the Pawnee native. I’d never considered that she wasn’t always that way, but in listening to her mock job interview for WSJ Magazine, that wasn’t always the case.

That’s not to say Poehler was some terrible person pre-Parks and Recreation; anyone who worked with her on SNL would vouch for her kindheartedness — especially Andy Samberg, who credits Poehler with him pursuing Brooklyn Nine-Nine. There’s no denying she’s become an even better person because of Leslie. As she went on to say:;

So what I like about her and what I try to remember, and why I think I deserve this job, she never thought it was lame to care about things. So when I catch myself not caring about things, I do think about her. Because she wouldn't have that.

Not being afraid to care deeply about things is definitely the biggest message I’ve taken away from watching Parks and Rec, and it’s nice to hear the same is true for Poehler. She’s definitely taken that to heart in how she carries herself on her podcast and even with her charity endeavors, like back in 2020 when the Parks and Rec cast reunited to benefit Feeding America.

#3714. Sir Patrick Stewart, Theater Titan and ‘Star Trek’ Captain, Dies at 86

Sir Patrick Stewart, the beloved actor of stage, screen, and television, died Wednesday following “a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia,” according to his representative, Kelly Bush Novak. The performer, best known in this and every other star system as Captain Jean-Luc Picard of the USS Enterprise, first appeared in the legendary role in September 1987. After seven seasons of television, four feature films, several video games, and site-specific interactive experiences, he returned to the character in the age of streaming, finally warping to retirement and surrounded by his crew, in January of 2020. He was 79 years old.

Stewart began his long and prosperous life in Yorkshire, England, as the youngest of three boys. His father was a World War II veteran, and, as Stewart discussed, suffered from post-traumatic stress disorder. Witnessing violence against his mother as a child, he said, led to Stewart’s later charity work for causes surrounding domestic violence.

He took theater classes in his youth and befriended a slightly older local lad, the actor-mountaineer Brian Blessed. He went on to study at the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School, a small, competitive conservatory that began with support from Sir Laurence Olivier, and boasts Daniel Day-Lewis, Olivia Colman, Jeremy Irons, Miranda Richardson, and many others as alumni.

In 1966, at age 26, Stewart joined the Royal Shakespeare Company, one of the most prestigious theater companies in Britain. During his time there, he appeared as the lead in The Life and Death of King John, as Oberon in A Midsummer Night’s Dream, and as Shylock in The Merchant of Venice, as well as more than 80 other roles, at the RSC’s main home in Stratford-upon-Avon, in London, and on tour. During this part of his career, he also appeared in supporting roles on television. The two most notable were the BBC production of I, Claudius, in which he played Emperor Tiberius’s double-crossing Praetorian guard Sejanus opposite a who’s who of British thespians (Derek Jacobi, John Hurt, Siân Phillips, Bernard Hill, John Rhys-Davies, Stewart’s old chum Brian Blessed, just to name a few), and as the evil mastermind Karla opposite Sir Alec Guinness in the adaptation of John Le Carré’s Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy and Smiley’s People.

As the 1970s turned to the 1980s, there were some film roles of note, including the part of Leodegrance in John Boorman’s Excalibur and Gurney Halleck in David Lynch’s version of Frank Herbert’s Dune. At one moment in the film, he leads a charge into battle clutching a cute li’l pug. (This same character, without the use of domesticated pets, was played by Josh Brolin in the more recent iteration.)

In 1986, with the original Star Trek still drawing good numbers in reruns and on videocassette, and with the feature films starring William Shatner and Leonard Nimoy doing well at the box office, Paramount thought it wise to update the series for television. Franchise creator Gene Roddenberry, who had worked on a “Phase II” Star Trek project in the late 1970s (which led, eventually, to the 1979 film) soon found himself at the drafting board for Star Trek: The Next Generation.

With a bridge crew of several writers and producers from what we now call The Original Series, the new version, set a little less than 100 years down the timeline, differentiated itself in a number of ways. The most notable change was reversing many of the attributes between the Captain and his first officer. Whereas Captain Kirk was a man of action, Captain Jean-Luc Picard was more cerebral, calculating, and cultured, sharing many characteristics with TOS’s half-Vulcan second-in-command, Mr. Spock. (TNG’s Commander Riker, played by Jonathan Frakes, was a bit more rough-and-tumble, and also likelier to woo interplanetary women.)

Patrick Stewart was not Roddenberry’s first choice (Belgian actor Patrick Bauchau, Yaphet Kotto, Roy Thinnes, and Dark Shadows’s Mitch Ryan were also in the mix). But in time, the not-too-well-known Shakespearean won out. When the casting was announced, a reporter suggested to Roddenberry that by the 24th century, in a time of faster-than-light starships, surely humankind would have found a cure for male pattern baldness, no? “No, by the 24th century, no one will care,” Roddenberry retorted, to the delight of bald guys everywhere.

As Stewart has repeated time and again, he took the gig thinking it was a doomed project, as no one would want to watch a retread of a classic. He figured he’d make a few quick bucks, secure some contacts, then head back to his real job on the British stage. He later called the decision to join Starfleet “the most important thing” in his career and his life.

But the first season of Star Trek: The Next Generation did not sail out of spacedock without some bumps. (Please don’t rewatch episode four, “Code of Honor,” if you know what’s good for you.) Though wanting to differentiate itself from TOS was the right move, some of the scripts could have used a little more derring-do, and the Picard character comes off at times as a little too cold. This unease was mirrored a bit behind the scenes, where Stewart experienced a little bit of culture clash.

Most of his fellow cast members were Americans who had worked in TV, like Night Court alum Brent Spiner. They were prone to goofing around in between takes, to the point that Stewart actually called a company meeting to scold them. It did not go over too well, but in time, Stewart began to loosen up. (This has now become a favorite thing for the gang to reminisce about during panels at Star Trek conventions, as everyone quickly became, and remained, good pals.)

The chemistry on the USS Enterprise (the Enterprise-D, if we’re getting specific) synched, and the show was a massive hit, making television history as a model for a successful first-run syndication. (If you happened to be a budding sci-fi nerd in central New Jersey that got both New York and Philly stations, it meant you could watch the show twice in the same weekend—not that I would know anything about that.)

From the first episode of TNG in late 1987, through a crossover to Star Trek: Deep Space Nine, and then feature films ending with 2002’s Star Trek: Nemesis, Stewart’s Picard saved the galaxy countless times with class, strength, and poise. Now is not the time to ask, “Who was the best captain?” But one can say, unequivocally, that Picard was the most quotable.

As TNG transitioned from television series to movies, Stewart, with more time on his hands, saw to it that his first role out of the gate would prove his range as an actor. As such, he costarred in the LGBTQ classic Jeffrey, based on Paul Rudnick’s play, as the flamboyant interior decorator Sterling. It may seem like nothing now, but, in 1995, to see a science fiction hero embracing a gay role was a bold move for progressivism.

In the 1990s, between Trek movies, Stewart played Captain Ahab in a USA Network adaptation of Moby Dick, led a one-man show version of A Christmas Carol, and played Prospero in The Tempest for the New York Shakespeare Festival. Then, in 2000, Stewart took on another clutch role in science fiction, Professor Charles Xavier in Bryan Singer’s version of X-Men.

As the schoolmaster/spiritual leader of Marvel’s mutant population, Stewart has played Professor X in eight features, most recently in Sam Raimi’s Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness. It was through the X-Men universe that he and Sir Ian McKellen forged their delightful and public friendship, which led to the two performing in Waiting for Godot together, and McKellen officiating at Stewart’s wedding to jazz singer Sunny Ozell in 2013.

In 2006, Stewart made the first of several returns to the Royal Shakespeare Company to play Mark Antony in Antony and Cleopatra. His most recent turn on the boards at his old haunt was 2011’s The Merchant of Venice, once again playing Shylock, for director Rupert Goold.

But after a slew of television guest spots (from Frasier to Extras) and lending his voice to various projects including several led by Seth MacFarlane, an album with classical pianist Emanuel Ax, and a profitable Pontiac campaign, he found himself going back to the future. Star Trek: Picard launched in 2020 with a rocky first two seasons before the ship righted itself for a final, triumphant season in 2023, shepherded by Terry Matalas, that reunited Stewart with the cast (and the more than 35-year-old ship) from The Next Generation.

Patrick Stewart was not Captain Jean-Luc Picard, but he brought him to life. Over 178 episodes of TNG (and countless novels and comic books that you can pretend are episodes in your head, not to mention daydreams) the French space explorer with the English accent was a beacon of righteousness and leadership. He accepted input and analysis from anyone in his crew, but felt no obligation to consensus when his mind was made up. He was bookish but also sexy and liked to keep his tunic straight.

As Stewart aged, he increasingly recognized the degree to which Star Trek meant something to millions (and would defend those hardcore fans when needed!) In 2010 he was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II. He won a Grammy in 1996 for best spoken word album for children (a recording of Peter and the Wolf) and in 2008 was nominated for a Tony for a production of Macbeth. He was nominated for four Emmys, though none of them for Star Trek.

During the coronavirus pandemic, he initiated a series on social media in which he read a new Shakespeare sonnet each day. We’ll conclude here with the final one.

#3713. How To Share Story Tips With Kotaku

Here at Kotaku, we strive to cut through the noise and nonsense and tell you real, interesting, and thought-provoking stories about the world of video games. In order to help us do that, we want people who know things about those video games and everything surrounding them to be able to talk to us securely and anonymously.

So weâve created a guide for anyone who wants to tip or share information with Kotaku, whether youâre a game developer, a customer service representative, a community leader, a PR representative, or a video game fan with a story to tell. The video game industry is shrouded in a culture of corporate silence that we do our best to penetrate every day, because we believe that people should have as much information as possible. So if you see or experience something that you think is important for people to know, or maybe just interesting, we want to hear from you, including in cases when you want your identity to be protected.

If you want to reach all of us, send your tips to: [email protected]

And if you want to send an e-mail to an individual Kotaku writer, find your favorite one on our masthead and shoot them a note.

Our tips inbox is only read by full-time staffers, and we check it every hour of every day. If you donât get a response, donât worry, weâve definitely seen it. And if you read this entire page and still arenât sure if you should send your tip, send it anyway. At worst, everyone at Kotaku will learn something new about the world of video games, and weâll be grateful for it.

But please do read the rest of the page first:

Weâre interested in news involving any aspect of gaming: game development, publishing, sales, things going on within games, things people are doing with games, all of it. Sometimes that means reporting on big cancelled projects or doing in-depth looks at chunks of video game history. Sometimes it means exposing malfeasanceâsharing stories about horrible work conditions at a game studio or reporting on a multinational company that isnât paying its staff on time. Sometimes it means answering big questions that everyoneâs asking, like why a game really keeps getting delayed over and over, or the events that led to a studio closure. We care about things that you yourself find interesting or surprising, and we want to help people know whatâs cool to play and what to avoid.

We primarily want gaming news, of course, and we care about it whether it comes from a gamer, a game-maker, or anyone else who gives a damn about video games. And if you have pictures, screenshots, video, or other first-hand evidence of whatever you want us to know about, thatâs a huge bonus.

We also, obviously, accept press releases, news about your cool indie game thatâs about to come out, pitches from PR to interview developers or preview or review games, and all the usual stuff. We recommend sending those to individual writers you have relationships with if possible, especially if you already know someone on staff is familiar with your game/genre/franchise. But if youâre just trying to reach us for the first time, the tips email is fine for that too.

Sometimes, you might want to share something with us, but want to remain anonymous because having your name attached to that information could come with consequences of some kind. Thatâs totally okay. In most cases, the journalist you speak to will still need to verify your identity (to prove youâd be in a position to know what youâre claiming to know), but will keep that information entirely to themselves if you prefer. We strictly do not share any information about anonymous sources with anyone for any reason.

In stories where we refer to sources who spoke to us anonymously, we will generally refer to those sources with as few details as possible. Often, that will just mean writing, âa source familiar with the matterâ or âan employee of [company]â or similar. Sometimes, some context clues will be necessary: for instance, if weâre writing about sexism at a studio, it may be important to identify the gender of our sources. We will always check with you first to make sure youâre comfortable with how youâre being referred to in the piece.

While we strictly do not share full articles with anyone outside of Kotaku prior to publication, we can on request go over your quotes with you after we speak to remind you of what was said and confirm there are no identifying details being used. We can also provide some general context about how the quotes are being used in the story, so you can help us confirm that our reporting is accurate to your understanding.

As a rule of thumb, you may not want to tell anyone that youâre talking to usâthe fewer people who know about any correspondence you may have with Kotaku, the more protected youâll be. Donât use your company e-mail account, any company-connected phone, work computer, or work WiFi network to contact us as an anonymous source. Instead, use a personal account or phone from home, or a public Wi-Fi network if you can do so safely. You can also reach most of our writers via Signal. Several of us have our Signal information in our social media bio pages, but if youâre looking for a specific writer, you can just email us directly and ask for our Signal name, no further context needed.

If the story youâd like to share with us would be improved by photos, screenshots, or other documentation, such records are often extremely helpful for us in corroborating a story and protecting your identity. If you can, itâs best to take pictures of photos or documents with a personal phone and send those, rather than the documents themselves. And when you send them to us, remove the metadata first. We do our own metadata scrubbing before we post leaked photos on Kotaku, but itâs best to be as safe as possible.

Similar to news tips, but different. While a lot of our stories are about game companies and creators, we also love writing about what gamers do.

Did you just play through Call of Duty without firing a shot? Are you one of the last dozen people playing the multiplayer in a game thatâs long since faded in popularity? Did you see someone pull off a crazy move in a Street Fighter tournament and happen to get video of it? Have you found a glitch no one knows about? Were you the person who figured out how to game the Steam summer sale? Did you make an incredible mod for your kids?

Maybe itâs not just you. Maybe youâve got a big Discord community dedicated to a game thatâs doing something neat. Or maybe youâre part of a subreddit thatâs very worked up about a niche update in the latest patch of your favorite game. Perhaps youâve got a local community putting on an in-person event surrounding something in a video game. Might be your guild in an MMO, your group chat, or maybe youâre still on forums.

We want to hear about all that stuff. Send it to tips. Send it to the staff. Just send it!

#3712. Days Gone studio's next PlayStation exclusive to be revealed and released in 2027, according to new report

Sony's Bend Studio, perhaps one of its lesser discussed development houses, has apparently been deep in development on its next title. The game is reportedly set to be announced in 2027, and released in the same year.

That's according to MP1st, citing "people aware of what's happening at Bend". Like Days Gone, Bend's next game is in third-person. The title is said to include co-op support, but no live service elements.

The report doesn't say whether the game is based on a new IP or an existing one, but it does state that it's not a sequel to Days Gone. The game is apparently "much further along in development" than we realise, which isn't entirely surprising considering Bend has been quiet for years.

The seven years since the release of Days Gone in 2019 have been tumultuous for Bend Studio. The developer revealed in 2022 its next project is a new IP that "builds upon the open-world systems of Days Gone" and includes multiplayer elements.

Two years later, a job post described a game in development at Bend as a triple-A live service project. That unannounced game was then cancelled in 2025, triggering a wave of layoffs at the studio that took place a few months later. Bend hasn't said a word since then.

It's now clear the studio hopped on its next project following the cancellation of that live service game. Seeing as 2026 is nearly over, we're not likely to be waiting much longer to see that mysterious game unveiled.

You might be thinking, if you're the optimistic sort, that today's official unveiling of The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel means that wheels are turning and things are happening and you're going to be off to Hammerfell soon—or at the very least, learning more about what's coming in Bethesda's next big RPG. Alas, in a follow-up post on social media, the studio made it clear that you shouldn't start holding your breath just yet.

"Thank you for 40 years of shared memories," Bethesda wrote. "We can't wait to make even more together with The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel. Development continues, and while it'll be some time before we're ready to share more, it feels great to finally reveal the name and location with you."

Thank you for 40 years of shared memories. We can’t wait to make even more together with The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel. Development continues, and while it’ll be some time before we’re ready to share more, it feels great to finally reveal the name and location with you.

"Some time" is obviously not a defined span, but I find that generally speaking it's a nicer, more politic way of saying "long time"—for instance, you could say it's been "some time" since Bethesda first announced the Elder Scrolls 6, and yeah, that's true. It was also eight freakin' years ago, and we've heard basically nothing since.

That is, very roughly, the same amount of time Bethesda needed to make the first Elder Scrolls game, Arena, as well as Daggerfall, Morrowind, the Morrowind expansions Tribunal and Bloodmoon, and the spinoff games Battlespire and Redguard. If you're (relatively) new to the series, eight years represents the span between Oblivion and The Elder Scrolls Online, a stretch interspersed by Skyrim and five major expansions: Knights of the Nine and Shivering Isles for Oblivion, and Dawnguard, Hearthfire, and Dragonborn for Skyrim.

Of course, Bethesda's had other things on the go over the past eight years too. Todd Howard said shortly after The Elder Scrolls 6 reveal that it was in pre-production, while Starfield was in full production. Starfield was Bethesda's top priority in the years leading up to its 2023 release; Howard later said that they'd just wanted to answer the fan question (are you making a new Elder Scrolls?) that came up every time they announced something else, like Starfield.

"Just pretend we didn't announce it," he joked. "Doesn't exist. No one's heard a word."How long Sentinel will take to get from here to launch is anybody's guess, although Bloomberg's Jason Schreier said on Bluesky that it's "still more than two years away." When questioned about his prediction, Schreier asserted that it's not a prediction at all, and that he knows "the time frame the game is targeting."

#3710. Remedy revenue soars by 226% following release of Control Resonant, the developer's fastest-selling game ever

Remedy - the developer behind the recently released Control Resonant - has released a scorcher of a quarterly financial report. It shows that following Resonant's release in September, the company's revenue surged by 226 percent, bringing in €39.6m in Q3.

This performance was described as "a defining milestone for the company" by CEO Jean-Charles Gaudechon. The company reported a €0.6m operating profit this quarter, a fair leap upwards from the €16.4m loss from this time last year.

There are some interesting highlights to this sudden surging performance. For one, the US made up nearly half of Control Resonant's players across PC and console, followed by Chinese-speaking regions and then the UK.

Perhaps most crucially is that nearly half of Control Resonant's players were entirely new to the franchise, with the company stating: "Reaching new players was a key goal for this game, and these early results indicate a growing audience for the franchise and for Remedy."

Control (2019) also saw a bump up in sales thanks to the release of Control Resonant, showing a stronger performance this quarter than the past two quarters this year as well as its comparison period (this quarter last year).

Remedy's CEO now believes the focus for the studio is to "get Resonant into the hands of more players." He continues to say the game has provided a solid foundation for growth as other projects (including the Max Payne 1 & 2 remake) are in the works. In short, things appear to be looking rather good for Remedy.

Control Resonant was an artistically impressive but critically divisive game. While many praised the series' adventure into third person action, some felt it had less of a narrative bite than its predecessor. Nonetheless the game quickly blasted past one million sales after launch.

#3709. Fan Who Went Viral Wishing To Stay Alive Long Enough To Play GTA 6 Has Passed Away

Jerry Fort, the GTA VI fan who went viral on TikTok for expressing his hope to live long enough to play the game, has passed away. As reported by Dexerto, his family confirmed the sad news, announcing that he passed on October 29th after complications following lung transplant surgery.

Earlier this year, Fort posted a video from his hospital bed titled “I just want to play GTA VI” in which he detailed his situation and prognosis. The video quickly went viral, garnering millions of views and tens of thousands of comments wishing him a speedy recovery and urging Rockstar Games to get in touch to make his wish come true. His family put up a Gofundme to raise money for a lung transplant and it quickly blew through its original $15,000 goal to reach over $100,000.

Fort and occasionally his sister posted regular updates to his account informing his followers of his progress, and it generally seemed like he was improving. In September, Fort went in for lung transplant surgery. After the surgery he developed an infection and after fighting the infection for several weeks, declining to go into hospice care, he finally succumbed.

After his plea to make it to GTA VI went viral, he put out a video thanking people for their support, promising to stream the game when he fully recovered. “That’s gonna be our goal as a community.”

The saga of It Ends With Us has lasted for years, with the two leads becoming synonymous with the book to screen adaptation and their long legal battle. Namely Blake Lively and Justin Baldoni, who have been battling in court due to allegations made about about the film (which is streaming with a Hulu subscription). The saga has taken another twist, as Baldoni reportedly sold his LA home in the wake of all the drama.

Blake Lively's complaints against Wayfarer Studios started a years-long legal battle between her and Justin Baldoni, who also directed and starred in It Ends With Us. Despite the pair issuing a joint statement and settling, the drama hasn't slowed down much. The latest update comes to us from Page Six, which claims that Baldoni sold his home in Los Angeles for over $2 million, after moving to Nashville in the midst of the drama with Lively.

The outlet claims that he sold the house back in August, and ended up making a profit of around one million dollars. Considering how wildly expensive lawyers fees were for both Lively and Baldoni, perhaps this sum will help to settle up with his representation.

The report also clarifies that the actor/producer/director still has a home on Ojai, so there are still some roots in California. Although it seems like his primary residence will be in Tennessee, where he'll presumably be able to operate with more anonymity than staying in California... especially as the It Ends With Us drama continues to make headlines.

As previously mentioned, the legal drama surrounding It Ends With Us has been going on for years, starting shortly after the movie arrived in theaters back in 2024. After his co-star's complaint Justin Baldoni filed his own defamation case, naming both Blake Lively and Ryan Reynolds in the process. Both of the movie's stars made allegations about what the other did on set, with the Jane the Virgin star claiming that Lively tried to take control of the movie. What's more, he also claimed that used famous friends like Taylor Swift to try and intimidate him in the midst of their drama.

The saga definitely captured the attention of fans, with the court of public opinion making their own judgements. It also seems to have negatively affect both of its stars' careers. For his part, Baldoni largely hasn't been working while dealing with his legal battle again Lively. Luckily for him that's about to change, as his company Wayfarer Studios will produce Gina Rodriguez's upcoming directorial debut. We'll just have to see if/when he gets in front of the camera again.

It Ends With Us is streaming now on Hulu. Baldoni didn't have projects on the 2026 movie release list, but maybe that'll change now that the drama is settling.

#3707. It looks like Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 had fewer active players at launch in the US compared to last year's Black Ops 7

It's been speculated for a while that Call of Duty may be losing its lustre. Although we don't have concrete data with detailed statistics for each game released in the last several years, there's an observable trend in player numbers that's hard to ignore.

US market analysis firm Circana published some data showing player engagement with Modern Warfare 4 following its launch, and compared them to those by Black Ops 7.

The data is based on Circana's proprietary Player Engagement Tracker, which tracks player activity in the US across Steam and PlayStation, and worldwide on Xbox. According to Circana analyst Mat Piscatella, 19 percent of players on PlayStation played Modern Warfare 4 in the week ending 24th October, compared to 17 percent on Xbox, and 4.2 percent on Steam.

With the exception of Steam, those numbers are down compared to last year's Black Ops 7, which saw 23 percent engagement on PlayStation, 29 percent on Xbox, and a meagre 1.5 percent on Steam during its launch week.

Call of Duty managed to land in the top 10 across all three platforms during the same week ending 24th October, per Circana. In fact, it sat just below Fortnite on PlayStation, which is a decent result.

The large drop in activity on Xbox could be explained by Modern Warfare 4's lack of a day-one release on Game Pass. Black Ops 7 was the second (and last) Call of Duty to launch on Game Pass day-and-date with its premium release. Game Pass availability typically boosts player numbers, though not always sales.

The drop on PlayStation is a little harder to explain, but could be a side effect of the incredibly successful Black Ops 1 & 2 ports released in the summer on PS4 and PS5, which captured lapsed players who may have simply lost interest in modern Call of Duty, regardless of the perceived quality of Modern Warfare 4.

Judging by the data we have access to, such as SteamDB numbers showing Modern Warfare 4's launch compared to Black Ops 7's and other recent releases, there's evidence this year's game perhaps isn't as popular as it could've been.

Indeed, even Activision's tenor when talking about Call of Duty first weekend sales has changed. The publisher issued a single statement following Modern Warfare 4's launch, through Xbox CEO Asha Sharma, which does not even mention the game by name.

"One of the most celebrated Call of Duty games in its 24-year history, and now $40bn in lifetime franchise revenue," Sharma wrote on X. "An incredible milestone. Congrats to the Activision team. And to the players, thank you for being with us."

Last year's Black Ops 7 post-launch statement sidestepped talk of sales and revenue entirely, insteading praising the "great response to the quality and depth of gameplay in Black Ops 7".

Welcome to FOV 90, an FPS column from staff writer Morgan Park. Every other week, I cover topics relevant to first-person shooter enjoyers, spanning everything from multiplayer and singleplayer to the old and the new.

Welcome back to a special election day edition of FOV 90, the only FPS column that insists American readers vote twice today—first on important videogame matters right here, then on crucial *gestures at everything else* matters at your designated polling place.

Today we return from a totally planned hiatus, during which the PC Gamer community settled both the best RTS unit and best horror games, to dispute an issue of far greater significance: The greatest FPS mode of all time. Round 2's matchups reflected an enthusiasm for classic team-based formats with a respectable turnout as well for modern arrivals like Battle Royale. I asked you to make some tough calls and you showed up.

Over 2,500 votes were cast across Round 2 matchups, and the results are in.

A decisive victory in each contest. Every mode I voted for came out on top, which I honestly didn't expect. Sure, TDM over Battle Royale makes sense, but an 82% majority tells me that the most popular shooter format of today has not usurped the classics among PC Gamer readers (same). But even so, this is where I expected Conquest (a chaotic fight over territory) to accept a humble defeat to Bomb Defusal (the gold standard of competitive PvP). I'm glad I was wrong!

Not as much comment sparring went down this time, but I would like to highlight one reader comment that got me thinking:

And here's how PC Gamer's staff reacted to the results:

"What's notable to me about the final four is that they mostly don't put individuals on the spot. In Infection, Battle Royale, and Bomb Defusal, you can wind up being the last survivor, with all the pressure on you to bring it home. That's not really the case in TDM, Conquest, Payload, or CTF, which usually allow unlimited respawns (or in the case of Conquest, end when respawns run out). CTF does require individual flag runner heroism, but as part of a team effort."

"The continued dominance of Payload is vexing to me: I've always thought it was Fine, but an all-conquering hero? Maybe I'm just sore it bodied Gun Game in the first round—I was a fan back when it was a modded Counter-Strike mode first and foremost. If Payload beats out the all time classic, Capture the Flag, this round, we may have to reexamine this whole "democracy" thing."

"CTF had its time, and was at its peak in the various iterations of Tribes, a context in which you could literally swoop in to snatch the banner. But I don't think it stands up if we're evaluating these as modern modes. Otherwise, it's tough to see Bomb Defusal fizzle—Counter-Strike's competitive mode holds up wonderfully as the premier FPS esport, which says a lot given that it's asymmetrical."

But alas, it's time to bury our dead and move on. Round 3 is on!

Read up on the matchups below and vote for your favorite. Round 3 voting closes on Sunday, November 8 at 11:59 PM PDT. The more votes we get, the more interesting the results, so tell your friends! Next week we'll be back to share the results and begin the FINALS.

AKA: Team Slayer (Halo) // Warfare (Hell Let Loose)

Intimate team-based action, or large-scale territory control?

AKA: It's always Payload and CTF, because they're perfect names

Two modes about escorting an object where the other team doesn't want it to go, but only one moves on.
