Final Fantasy VII RebirthFinal Fantasy VII RemakeSaleSwitch 2

Final Fantasy VII Remake Intergrade and Rebirth both came to Switch 2 earlier this year and they are currently just $8 each. That is a ridiculously low price for two very good ports of two excellent RPGs.

#3664. Resident Evil Director Reacts To Backlash: “I Should Have Known Better”

Resident Evil is a huge success at the box office, recently surpassing $400 million globally. It's also received fantastic review scores. But hardcore fans of the game series took issue with the film and its direction because it did not contain any storylines or characters from the source material. Director Zach Cregger never intended to, instead opting for his own original story that is set in the world of Resident Evil. Now, Cregger has spoken more about the fallout, saying he became "frustrated at the conversation" around his movie and specifically how it "didn't have anything to do with the movie."

He said on The Town that the conversation from the hardcore Resident Evil fanbase was that the movie didn't live up to their standards, even though Cregger never said he was trying to make a movie that did that.

He said he really loves and is proud of the movie he made. At the same time, Cregger admitted, "I should have known better" about how fans of the game series might react. Anyone who has been on the internet and engaged with anything related to gaming knows how intense hardcore gaming fans can be about even the seemingly smallest of issues, but Cregger said he overlooked this for reasons he doesn't fully understand.

"I should have understood that that was going to be the case," Cregger said about the blowback. Cregger previously said he was naive to think gamers would embrace him and his idea for the Resident Evil movie.

Cregger previously said he would never make another franchise movie after Resident Evil, but he's softened somewhat, saying on the podcast that he has a "never say never" attitude about it. Asked if Cregger's anti-franchise stance might limit his job opportunities in the future, Cregger said that after Barbarian and Weapons, he feels like he is "playing with house money."

Cregger said he's basically already won in life and the rest of his career is gravy. He said he goes into his projects now thinking it could be the last film he ever makes, and he's OK with that. "I'm going to swing for the f**king fences," he said. "I'm going to pour it all out to make this as good as I am capable of making it. And whatever happens, whether it makes a lot of money or no money, I just have to make sure I left it all on the court. And if that's the end, then I've had an amazing run."

Cregger is, of course, not finished making movies. His next film is the deep space sci-fi movie The Flood, starring Jennifer Lawrence. He said in the interview that it's his biggest-budget movie ever; previously, that record belonged to Resident Evil (a reported $75 million before marketing costs). Cregger said he shouldn't admit this publicly, but he believes there are real benefits to making movies on lower budgets, in part so a filmmaker like himself has to get creative as he works against constraints.

The Resident Evil movies are produced by Constantin Films, which bought the rights back in the '90s and has retained them ever since. After Welcome to Raccoon City flopped, Constantin planned to put the film franchise on ice ... until Cregger showed up with a pitch.

In addition to The Flood, Cregger is producing the next Weapons movie, which is the spin-off, Aunt Gladys.

#3662. Marilyn Monroe and Arthur Miller’s Tragic Love Story

“I think you’re the saddest girl I ever met.”

“You’re the first man that ever said that. I’m usually told how happy I am.”

This exchange, from The Misfits, written by Arthur Miller, shows Marilyn Monroe drawing closer to something other than the “dumb blonde” persona for which Hollywood praised her.

After all, the actor—who was born in Los Angeles in 1926 and died in the City of Angels in 1962 at the age of 36—wanted to be taken seriously as a performer. She never fully identified with the image Hollywood created for her. She spent her limited free time enjoying uncharacteristic pastimes, as evidenced by one of her most famous photographs, which depicts her reading James Joyce’s Ulysses while donning a striped tank top, black shorts, and a deep, melancholic gaze.

Marilyn Monroe reads a book in her room at the Hotel Ambassador in midtown Manhattan, March 1955.

“A sex symbol becomes a thing. I just hate to be a thing,” said Monroe to Life magazine in 1962, reflecting on her strained relationship with Hollywood.

Miller, who was born in New York in 1915 and passed away in 2005, initially believed he would be a good partner for Monroe, whose life was marked by great successes, but also abandonment and her unfortunate inability to have children—one of the most painful issues for Monroe.

Monroe and Miller first met in 1950, when he was in Los Angeles with director Elia Kazan. It was Kazan who introduced them.

Monroe and Miller began talking, and he emphasized her potential to become a dramatic actor on New York stages. He struck a chord.

In the mid-1950s, the star left Hollywood and moved to New York to study, attending The Actors Studio and working with Lee Strasberg. She met with Miller again in the Big Apple, and in 1955, they began dating seriously, joining two seemingly distant worlds.

Marilyn Monroe and playwright Arthur Miller play with his dog Hugo,at Miller’s summer home on June 25, 1956.

Monroe felt respected by him, unlike the way she felt in Hollywood, which she once called “an overcrowded brothel, a merry-go-round with beds for horses,” in her unfinished memoir, My Story.

Miller, who had won the Pulitzer Prize in 1949 for Death of a Salesman, was captivated by her and ended his failing marriage.

The subsequent marriage between Monroe and Miller—her third marriage, his second—took place on June 29, 1956, in White Plains, New York. A few days later, a private Jewish ceremony was also held, following the actor’s conversion to Judaism.

The first major rift in their marriage stemmed from ongoing tension between public and private life. Miller wanted a more secluded, domestic life; Monroe wanted a family, but she was not willing to give up the career she had so painstakingly built.

For the 1957 film The Prince and the Showgirl—directed by and starring Laurence Olivier, with Monroe as the female lead and coproducer—the actor and her husband moved to England, where tensions rose.

Arthur Miller and Marilyn Monroe after their wedding.

Monroe found some of Miller’s notes, in which he expressed disappointment with their marriage and admitted to sometimes feeling embarrassed around his friends in the cultural world.

It was one of the hardest moments in their relationship: Monroe discovered that the man who seemed to recognize her talent and intelligence also viewed her through the very same lens from which she was trying to free herself.

In her own notebooks, she reflected on her fear of becoming “someone’s wife” and losing her independence.

Miller would later say that he wrote very little during the years of his marriage.

Monroe, meanwhile, was struggling to become a mother. During her marriage, she experienced a miscarriage, an ectopic pregnancy, and another spontaneous termination of pregnancy.

On the set of The Prince and the Showgirl, her difficulties increased: She often arrived late, struggled to work consistently, and her relationship with Laurence Olivier became strained.

In the background, Miller faced a trial, as he had refused to name Communist Party members and sympathizers. He was convicted of contempt of Congress in 1957, but the conviction was overturned the following year.

Marilyn Monroe and her former husband Arthur Miller as they leave Doctors Hospital on August 10, 1957, after she recovered from a 10-day hospital stay following an ectopic pregnancy.

Despite Monroe publicly expressing her support for her husband, the cracks in their marriage turned into chasms. Arguments, a lack of trust, disillusionment, drugs, alcohol, all of it became too difficult to contain.

The point of no return was another feature film, The Misfits, written by Miller for Monroe.

The desert setting where it was filmed didn’t help. Amid hellish temperatures, Monroe and Miller were no longer on speaking terms, even though they were staying at the same hotel. Intermediaries were needed just to get them to communicate.

It was during this shoot that Miller met the photographer Inge Morath, whom he would later marry in February 1962.

They divorced shortly after The Misfits was released in theaters.

After The Misfits, Monroe went through one of the most difficult periods of her life. In 1961 she was admitted to the Payne Whitney Psychiatric Clinic in New York. Joe DiMaggio intervened to have her transferred to another facility.

Marilyn Monroe’s photo shoot at Hollywood agent Johnny Hyde’s backyard in Beverly Hills, California, 1957.

Before her death, Monroe nevertheless continued to work, seek roles, and imagine a life different from the one others intended for her.

In a 1988 interview that aired on the Italian network Rai, journalist and writer Enzo Biagi asked Miller: “How do you want to remember Marilyn Monroe?”

He replied: “She made everyone believe she was very happy, but I didn’t believe it. She was very depressed, but she had the extraordinary talent of being able to mask her state of mind. She wore a mask because she was suffering too much. She was completely unable to cope with her depression, but she had been an abused child. She was looking for someone to save her.”

Originally published by Vanity Fair Italia.

#3661. Gears Of War: E-Day’s Apparent $500 Million Budget May Not Tell The Full Story – Report

How much does a true console exclusive cost to make today? If recent reports are to be believed, Gears of War: E-Day had a production cost $500 million, but there's more to that figure than just a single game.

That's according to Windows Central writer Jez Corden, who says he spoke with multiple sources familiar with the story behind the half-billion dollars paid over several years to The Coalition while it was working on Gears of War: E-Day. The studio emerged from the COVID-19 pandemic as a Swiss Army Knife developer that assisted not only on several Xbox games, but also worked on the technology powering them.

As Corden explained, The Coalition worked with Epic Games on the oThe Matrix Awakens and Alpha Point tech demos for Unreal Engine 5 demonstrations, and used that knowledge to help other developers in the Xbox Games Studio portfolio. The Coalition reportedly worked for over 18 months on a prototype game that was eventually canceled, assisted on Avowed, Hellblade 2, Clockwork Revolution, State of Decay 3, Grounded, and Grounded 2, and even contributed to the upcoming StarCraft at Blizzard.

Once Mike Crump was appointed studio head, development on Gears of War: E-Day reportedly kicked into full gear. That makes for a busy developer, and one that brings a lot of institutional knowledge to Xbox with its work on Unreal Engine 5, which is one of the most popular engines for video game development. "I can't help but feel like the '$500 million' figure being shared around internally is being used to justify potential cuts, layoffs, or worse, a studio closure targeting The Coalition. Perhaps to 'soften the blowback,' should Microsoft target the studio. For what it's worth, I've not heard that Xbox is planning to close The Coalition," Corden added.

Gears of War: E-Day has reportedly not sold well either, but this can be attributed to various factors. It was only released for PC and Xbox Series X|S, is also available through Xbox Game Pass, and it happened to launch during an exceptionally busy time, as the last couple of months have been loaded with several major game releases, creating a lot of competition for a person's attention and money.

Circana analyst Mat Piscatella recently commented on the game, saying that making Gears of War: E-Day exclusive to Xbox "hasn’t made any difference" in terms of selling more Xbox consoles.

#3660. We Finally Know Who Made The Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Remake

Fans have speculated on which studio is leading the development of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake since it was first announced, and a new Ask the Developer feature from Nintendo appears to give us the answer.

The interviewees in Nintendo's online feature include longtime Zelda producer Eiji Aonuma and several members of Nintendo Entertainment Planning & Development (EPD) Production Group No. 3, which is the team behind the mainline Zelda games. In other words, the usual Zelda people are making the new Zelda game, as opposed to another studio like Monolith Soft or Grezzo.

Those other two studios have come up in fan discussions about the Ocarina of Time remake, due to their respective histories contributing to the Zelda franchise. Grezzo was behind the 3DS remakes of Ocarina of Time and Majora's Mask, along with the Switch remake of Link's Awakening. The studio also co-developed Echoes of Wisdom with EPD No. 3.

Monolith Soft, the Nintendo subsidiary behind the Xenoblade games, has taken more of a support role with Zelda games in recent years. The studio is credited with contributing to Skyward Sword, Breath of the Wild, and Tears of the Kingdom.

Fans had guessed that either or both studios were working on the Ocarina remake for Switch 2, theorizing that EPD No. 3 was working on a new, mainline Zelda game. Neither Monolift Soft nor Grezzo are mentioned in the first two parts of the Ask the Developer feature (parts 3 and 4 will be published on November 3), but it's still entirely possible that they could be involved in the production as support studios. We'll have to wait and check the credits when the game launches on November 5.

For now, be comforted knowing that development on the Ocarina remake is being led by veterans of the beloved series, satisfying the fan desire to know exactly who's making these Nintendo games.

CBS confirmed on Monday, November 2, that Shantel VanSanten is returning in an upcoming episode. Her character, Special Agent Nina Chase, will reunite with husband Stuart Scola (John Boyd) for a case involving the murder of an online influencer.

The team must use Nina’s help to intercept the criminal — who is on the Most Wanted list — before he disappears. While Nina is there to assist Scola at work, her return comes as she is considering a new position.

During Monday’s episode, Maggie (Missy Peregrym) and OA (Zeeko Zaki) asked Scola whether Nina is getting her own task force. Scola confirmed the news, but it wasn’t until later in the episode that he offered more details.

“Job’s in San Diego,” he said. “She got the offer four days ago. Everything she ever wanted. She’d have to move to California.”

Scola hinted he was considering making the move with Nina since they are now married and share a child.

“I don’t know. She’s worked so hard for this,” he added. “Her whole career. But we have a life here. We’d have to uproot everything. Just the sacrifice that’s needed if Nina takes this gig, I just don’t know if our family would survive that.”

He continued: “I told her not to take it. I said she shouldn’t accept the promotion.”

Despite his concerns, Scola left Nina a voicemail, in which he said, “Hey, it’s me. I’ve been thinking more about San Diego. I think you should take the job. It’s worth it. We’ll figure it out, OK? I love you.”

The actress was glad she could come back so Nina and Scola could tie the knot on FBI.

“[It is] OK to go through things and allow it to change you and to transform your ideas about life or love or relationships,” she said about the fictional couple’s journey. “I think that it was really special.”

VanSanten didn’t rule out future cameos at the time.

“Once you’re in this world, I feel like, you know, I’m [a] phone call away,” she added. “And we’re married. So for now, we’re stuck until the next iteration.”

#3658. Devs Are Blaming A Flood Of AI Slop On Steam For Delaying Their Games

November is, to put it lightly, nuts for video games. World of Warcraft: Forever launches tomorrow. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time will be out just a few hours after that. And a short two weeks after that, the juggernaut arrives: GTA 6. So as you might imagine, dozens of indie games are trying to get their releases out now, before these heavy hitters show up and suck all the air out of the room, monopolizing the time of content creators and players who might otherwise pay attention to smaller projects. But the folks behind a lot of those indie games are now worried they might be forced to launch right in the middle of that AAA maelstrom, thanks to what they believe to be a major bottleneck going on internally at Valve; one they think is caused by a flood of AI slop games.

Throughout October, multiple indies have posted on social media suggesting that their approvals process on Steam was taking longer than usual. Normally, Valve says it expects a 3-5 day waiting period when a developer submits a game for approval to appear on the Steam store. Valve then might get back to the developer with any issues it has, and it’s another few days to review again. Once Valve considers any such issues resolved, the game can then be published on the storefront. For all this, Valve specifically advises developers, “you’ll want to submit your page for review at least 7 business days before you want it live to account for potential changes you’ll need to make.”

Except recently, seven business days hasn’t cut it. Throughout October, a number of indie developers have posted on social platforms sharing that their reviews are taking two or three weeks or more to complete for no discernible reason.

There’s Caravarn Carnage: Fruity Road, for instance, which finally made it through Steam approvals on November 1 after submitting on October 16:

Hi @Steamworks, my games build has been stuck in review since October 16, beyond the usual 3-5 business days. I've contacted support but haven't received an update on the build review.

Ashen Legacy submitted on October 15, and was finally approved on November 1, coming in hot ahead of a planned November 6 release date:

Oh my god! My first submission was rejected, and Iâve already had to wait over two weeks. The scariest thing right now isnât the threat of AI-generated game clonesâitâs the wait for Steamâs review process. Itâs a race to see whose game gets approved first, and with my scheduledâ¦ pic.twitter.com/rgbgwK8PVE

— Ashen Legacy | Wishlist on Steam (@VerStudiovn) October 31, 2026

Lacey’s Flash Games was recently forced into a delay; it finally came out on Halloween, four days late:

And Wheel Make It was forced to launch three weeks late:

Wheel Make It has been unintentionally delayed while we're waiting on @Steam's approval.

The game was submitted for review 2 weeks ago, and was rejected because they couldn't figure out how to access local co-op (you literally just share a keyboard…)

The re-review has beenâ¦ pic.twitter.com/jLvB6QHZvK

— 2 Left Thumbs (@2_left_thumbs) October 12, 2026

Here’s a statement from Mira, one of the developers of the similarly-in-limbo Cubic Earth, provided to Kotaku:

We’re a small team, and we’ve spent a long time building up to getting our debut Early Access title, Cubic Earth, out into the world. Having it derailed last minute has been incredibly disheartening. Despite our best effort to follow Valve’s established processes and adherence to their stated timelines, our game now has no known launch window.

We’ve received a number of player complaints and questions across the Steam Community and YouTube, wondering why the game did not launch at the stated time. To make matters worse, organic traffic to our store page from Steam features has dropped off completely, and what was shaping up to be a promising Early Access launch now feels more like an anxiety inducing nightmare.

We’re hoping that this can be resolved as painlessly as possible, and trying to keep our eyes on the future!

Earlier today, I spoke at length to another impacted developer: Alfred Kamon, director of Studio Daimon, which is making Food Devils. Food Devils was supposed to launch today. It won’t be doing that, though, because it’s still awaiting Steam approval after being submitted way back on October 12.

Kamon says he first started to wonder if something was wrong about a week after the submission, with Valve still silent. On October 24, he followed Steam’s published advice for what to do if response was too slow: he submitted a support ticket. On the 26th, Valve responded with a concern about sexual content in the game, to which Kamon immediately replied in an attempt to resolve the issue. Now, seven days after that, he’s still waiting for a reply. Valve also responded to his support ticket, essentially telling him to wait for the review team to get back to him. (Kotaku has seen all of these messages between Kamon and Valve).

Kamon tells me that from his perspective, Studio Daimon did everything right in order to launch on time. Even with Valve having an issue with content, he says that in the past such problems have only taken 2-3 days to resolve, and he had prepared for that. He had not prepared for three weeks of waiting…and counting. He can’t even provide full game keys to reviewers until approvals are done (beta keys can and have gone out).

“Just before the release, everyone is crunching a lot just to finish everything, to do QA, to polish and to prepare all the content,” he said. “So everyone in the team maybe even stayed up late or even during weekends. It was very, very hard. And despite everything, I think it’s sad because everyone made so many sacrifices to be here now today, and we still couldn’t make it.”

What’s really ironic is that Food Devils‘ original release date was actually supposed to be November 5, but 24 hours before the team planned to announce it, Ocarina of Time planted its flag that same day. So the team moved it up. “Oh, no, we are not releasing on the same day as Zelda,” Kamon said. Of course, now there’s a solid chance they might.

I asked Kamon if it made sense to hold the game even longer, maybe into early December. After all, following Ocarina of Time is GTA 6. It’s a terrible month to release a small indie game, and Food Devils was originally getting in just barely under the wire. But Kamon tells me that’s not an option.

Studio Daimon is a small studio: just nine people, based in Italy, working on Food Devils for the last four years. It’s made one other game before, Path of the Midnight Sun, and it’s not exactly rolling in cash. Kamon tells me that the studio really needs the money from sales of Food Devils before the end of the year, and Steam pays out on a one-month delay. If Food Devils can’t launch soon, the studio might be in trouble financially.

Why is all this happening? No one knows for sure. Valve hasn’t said. We reached out to the company for comment, and were told a blog post is coming sometime later today, but we were not briefed on its contents and aren’t sure when it will drop; we’ll update when it does. Impacted developers have a theory about what’s happening, though: they think it’s an AI slop problem.

As of mid-October, more games have been released on Steam in 2026 than in all of 2025, with two and a half months to go. And in October alone, around 4,000 games were released on the platform, with nearly 50 percent of them disclosing some use of generative AI in development. That’s a lot of games coming through very, very fast, the speed aided by the ability of generative AI to churn out game-shaped things quickly. Developers suspect that, given these numbers, Valve is struggling to keep up with the sudden influx of submissions, and smaller studios without the clout to ask Valve to expedite their games are suffering for it. But without word from Valve, no one can prove that’s what’s really happening.

The thing is, ValveÂ hasÂ acknowledged that the platform has some issue with AI slop. It finally made a statement last week, after over 8,000 demos flooded Steam Next Fest last month, alongside a report that a developer was extorted by someone threatening to make an AI clone of their project, as well as several developers admitting publicly that they hesitated to release game demos for fear of having their games cloned. But that statement was just that people at Valve didn’t want to be “gatekeepers telling developers which tools they should or shouldn’t use.”

Valve’s Marc Wilkinson also said, “We are fully aware of the situation, and a significant number of people are thinking about how to solve this problem.” But as much as one might appreciate how difficult it may be to figure out how to regulate AI, at the moment, a number of developers are actively suffering with no clear path to relief.

At this point, all Kamon wants is for Food Devils to be approved as soon as possible. He did say it would be nice to get some increased visibility on Steam to make up for this situation, since his release plans have now been all messed up through no fault of his own. And he wishes Valve would be transparent about how long the review process will take.

“I can also sympathize with those who have to review all these games,” he says. “But as a dev, at least I would like some honesty in the UI when you submit a game. Tell us it may take weeks. Just don’t promise us three to five days because then we make plans around the release date. We create hype. We announce everything. People are happy that the game is releasing and in the end, it doesn’t.”

#3653. Claude Code Just Got A New Rule: Stop Copying Other People’s Games

AI clones and vibe-coded copycat games have become a huge headache for developers recently, but it looks like an update to Anthropic's Claude Code's "rules" has been pushed out. Listed under "tengu_heron_brook," the tweak to the AI now directs it not to copy games and assets, and users cannot disable this setting.

Spotted by Chasm on X (via Game Developer), the full rule reads, "Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Don't build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original". Anthropic's Addy Osmani added that "two sentences" were added to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5, to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game, as "using Claude to infringe IP " is against the company's policy. "Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working. We'll continue to iterate to ensure we're striking the right balance."

AI clones have been running rampant for months now, as the tools have let pretty much anyone crank out copies of successful games in surprisingly little time compared to traditional methods of cloning a successful piece of work. This all came to a head during Steam Next Fest last month, when the demo showcase was flooded with low-effort games and AI slop. This has also led several developers to cancel demos outright, fearing bad actors could take the code, whip up a copy in Claude, and release it before their game ships.

Valve has vaguely mentioned that it's "aware of the situation" and that "a significant number of people are thinking about how to solve" the problem. At the same time, Valve has encouraged developers to focus on building communities and support for games, which isn't exactly an ideal solution. Creating a community around a game takes time, whereas AI slop clones can be generated fast enough to capitalize on virality, and in an ideal situation, make a quick buck for the prompter on the other end--just look at all the video games about needles in haystacks that have popped up recently, copying the viral success of Needle in a Haystack Simulator, which isn't out yet.

The rampant reverse-engineering got so bad that the creator behind Needle in a Haystack Simulator, NasNakarus, poked fun at it by teasing a joke mode for the game where players will have to sift through piles of cloned games to find the original.

While tweaking Claude is good news, it doesn't mean developers are out of the woods yet. Claude prompters will likely look for ways to work around the new restrictions, and if they're unsuccessful, other AI agents are available without the same safeguards.

Grey's Anatomy is one of the most legendary medical dramas of all time, and we're currently in its whopping 23rd season on ABC (and streaming with a Hulu subscription). The beloved medical drama is till going strong, but many fans like to look back at its glory days. Late actor Eric Dane famously played Mark Sloane/ McSteamy during that time, and excerpts from his posthumous memoir got honest about his struggles during that time.

McSteamy is one of the most beloved Grey's character of all time, in no small part thanks to the charisma and heart that Dane brought to the role. In his recently released memoir My Book of Days (via EW) he wrote about an injury and reliance on painkillers resulted in him deteriorating during his time at Seattle Grace Hospital. He wrote:

My body goes to shit. I drop to 170, my face caves in, my eyes cloud, I look gaunt; shit, I look like a drug addict. You can tell. I can tell. My attitude on set changes. I’m no longer bubbly, the fun guy, a ringleader in laughs. I don’t act out. I don’t throw tantrums or chairs. I go the other way. I bring everything inside. I dissolve.

What a heartbreaking recollection. While Grey's fans were still head over heels in love with Sloan, Dane was having a private struggle with his health and substances that was making his job difficult. Rather than acting out he felt himself "dissolving", and not letting it impact this coworkers. Indeed, Grey's Anatomy stars wrote tributes to the late actor following his tragic death in February.

Later in his memoir, the Euphoria star does mention that his coworkers noticed the change in him. He wrote about the dynamic he felt at the time, in a section which reads:

I can’t help it. I feel other members of the cast looking at me. They’re my friends. My work family. No. My family. They don’t judge me. They don’t look angry. They look concerned. They look sad.

It's tough to hear how Eric Dane was struggling during this time, and how he was being so private about it while bringing McSteamy to life. He didn't want to bother his co-workers and chosen family, but they noticed that something was going on. That includes the one and only Shonda Rhimes, who did offer to help the Last Ship actor. As he wrote:

I tell her I’m dealing with it. I lie to her. I lie to myself. I suck it up. Fight through it. I don’t want to be Shonda’s burden. I don’t want to be a problem. But I am. I am a problem.

Clearly Eric Dane took the time to reflect on his years on Grey's Anatomy, and the struggles he was dealing with at the time. In his book he was able to speak honestly about his issues, and take responsibility for being a "problem." It's a powerful testament, one that might help inspire readers who are dealing with similar issues.

New episodes of Grey's Anatomy air Thursdays on ABC as part of the 2026 TV schedule. Folks who want to re-watch Dane's iconic tenure as McSteamy can do so on both Hulu and Netflix. Although after hearing about his experience, it might hit differently.

After working in administrative theater for a year in New York, he started as the Weekend Editor at CinemaBlend. He's since been able to work himself up to reviews, phoners, and press junkets-- and is now able to appear on camera with some of his favorite actors... just not as he would have predicted as a kid. He's particularly proud of covering horror franchises like Scream and Halloween, as well as movie musicals like West Side Story. Favorite interviews include Steven Spielberg, Spike Lee, Jamie Lee Curtis, and more.

#3651. GTA 6 Buying Guide: Get Ready For Sticker Shock

Rockstar's GTA 6 finally releases on November 19, and if you're looking to play the game, you'll also need a console--and those are more expensive than ever. Here's a quick buying guide to help you understand what you need and how much the items will cost. 

A console

First, you'll need a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X|S console. The least expensive option for buying a new system outright is the Xbox Series S, which costs $500. Unfortunately, that's $200 more expensive than the system cost at launch in 2020--there are a number macroeconomic and AI factors that drove prices up significantly.

A new Xbox Series X, meanwhile, costs $750 for a system with no disc drive, or $800 for a console with a disc drive. GTA 6 is not available on a disc, but having a disc drive may still be important to you for other games and media like DVDs and Blu-rays. 

Switching to PlayStation, the least expensive system on Sony's side is the $600 digital edition, scaling up to $900 for a PS5 Pro (with a disc drive). PS5 Pro, as the most powerful of these options, is likely to provide the best experience from a technical and graphical standpoint, although the gameplay itself should be identical across all platforms.

These are all prices for brand-new units, but Sony offers certified refurbished PS5 consoles starting at $500. A certified refurbished Xbox Series S, meanwhile, goes for $400. These are the prices from Sony and Microsoft directly, but you can find secondhand consoles at a variety of other retailers, along with places like eBay, Facebook Marketplace, and Craigslist. As usual, check your local or preferred retailer to see the latest prices.

New and certified refurbished consoles come with everything you need--including the system, controller, and power cords. You will need a TV or monitor, but the odds are good that if you're looking to play GTA 6, you probably already have one. 

People on platforms outside PlayStation and Xbox are out of luck, as GTA 6 has not been announced for Switch 2 or PC. A PC edition is expected to release in early 2027, but there is no word on a Switch 2 version. 

The game

To play GTA 6 you will need to buy GTA 6. The game's standard edition goes for $80, with its Ultimate Edition selling for $100. As mentioned, the game is not available on a disc. That being said, retailers are selling the $80 edition in stores, though you only get a code in the box. The $100 edition appears to be exclusive to digital storefronts.

The $100 Ultimate Edition includes loads of extras, including a variety of cosmetics and even in-game shops that people who buy the $80 edition cannot access. Since GTA 6 is a digital-exclusive game, there is no reason to worry about units selling out, but if you do want to preorder, you get the Vintage Vice City Pack and a free month of GTA+.

GTA 5 launched at $60 back in 2013--adjusted for inflation, that's about $85 today.

You will also need an internet connection to install GTA 6, since it's a digital only game. It's a beefy one, too, weighing in at a reported 201GB. Thankfully, preloading begins on November 12, a full week before the game launches. That means you'll be able to begin downloading it early in the hopes of being ready to go on November 19.

November 12 is also when GTA 6's code-in-a-box copies will be available to buy at physical stores. You're not getting a week of early access, though, as the game does not unlock fully until November 19.

Do you need PS Plus or Game Pass?

GTA 6 is a strictly single-player game, and as such, you likely will not need PlayStation Plus or Xbox Game Pass to play. Rockstar has yet to confirm this, however. 

Rockstar is surely going to release a new version of GTA Online at some point--some believe that will happen in early 2027. And at that point, you'll likely need a membership. But for launch, there is no online or multiplayer support, so we don't think a subscription to PS Plus or Game Pass would be required. 

Why no disc?

Neither Rockstar nor studio owner Take-Two have provided a reason for GTA 6 being a digital exclusive, but the answer seems pretty obvious: It's all about money. Rockstar makes more money from digital game sales, and having no disc eliminates the secondhand market. 

“A disc can be resold or rented a hundred times, and Rockstar earns nothing after that first sale," Rhys Elliott of Alinea Analytics said. 

The code-in-a-box strategy for physical games has been around for a long time already, and while people might complain online about the lack of a physical edition of GTA 6, the game is going to sell phenomenally no matter what, Mat Piscatella of Circana says.

Beyond these factors, consumer spending patterns have trended increasingly toward digital since the early 2010s. GTA 6 is such a large game in terms of its file size, so making it digital-exclusive also saves Rockstar and Take-Two money by not needing to print a second disc, if one was ever needed.

#3650. Is This the Last Dance for Spain’s Prime Minister, Pedro Sánchez?

On September 23, Maricarmen Abascal, a partially disabled 87-year-old woman, was evicted from the apartment she rented in Madrid, where she had lived her entire life. Suffering from exhaustion caused by the long struggle to keep her home and then her subsequent eviction, she was admitted to a hospital. That same day, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez addressed the United Nations General Assembly in New York, an international forum where he has often promoted his foreign policy agenda, beginning with his first visit in 2018, when the politician who had been given the nickname Mr. Handsome met many of his counterparts around the globe. While Abascal would never return to her home (she died on October 7), and her eviction sparked widespread public outrage, Sánchez spoke of reforming international organizations, criticized the United States and Israel, and called for reining in the “tech oligarchs” at the helm of social media platforms and artificial intelligence companies: “The future of our sons and daughters must take precedence over the financial interests of these techno-oligarchs.”

No one in Spain paid attention to the speech: Abascal’s eviction sparked social unrest in a country that boasts of being the fastest-growing in Europe in terms of GDP, a fact on which the Banco de España and the International Monetary Fund agree. This has positioned the country as one of the leading economies in the eurozone, with unemployment having fallen to historic lows, according to official figures. In macroeconomic terms, the country has consistently appealed to international investors during Sánchez’s eight years in office, with foreign investment having grown 34% since 2018, according to calculations by the Ministry of Economy. It’s possible that the Spanish economy is experiencing its best period of growth since the country’s return to democracy in the mid-1970s. However, inflation, housing affordability, and low wages—the minimum wage has risen from 735 euros to 1,221 euros, but has failed to boost salaries broadly—are taking a toll on this economic boom.

And, among voters, there’s a sense of mismanagement during this legislative term. There was the migration crisis in Ceuta, a Spanish enclave on the North African coast that saw the sudden arrival of more than 72,000 migrants in late July. (Ceuta has just over 83,000 residents.) The crisis was not enough to get Sánchez to cut short his vacation. It revealed clashes between the ministers of defense and the interior, and it has taken nearly three months for the situation to be brought fully under control. Political scientist and university professor Lluís Orriols noted in El Periódico that the government had come out “badly” in its handling of crises such as the one in Ceuta and the eviction of Abascal—problems compounded by “legislative paralysis” (the government has managed to pass fewer than 40 laws in this legislative session, down from more than 100 in the previous one) and “corruption.” He asserted that only the strength of the economy had prevented “a government in shambles.”

After elections in 2023, Sánchez managed to secure another term, but without a clear left-wing majority, he had to rely on the support of several right or center-right nationalist parties without a legislative pact, which led to numerous parliamentary defeats. The coalition has failed to provide Spain with an effective government. The international landscape has not been particularly favorable either. Sánchez has gradually lost his key allies: That group of young, charismatic left-wing leaders who seemed to set the global agenda and had a special rapport with the Spanish leader have long since left power—the photos showing the admiration for Sánchez from Sanna Marin of Finland, Justin Trudeau of Canada, and Jacinda Ardern of New Zealand are now a thing of the past. His rapport with other European leaders such as Emmanuel Macron, a relationship marked by effusive camaraderie since way back in 2018, is of little use now that France is in turmoil and advocates for a return to austerity are gaining power in Europe. Even his relationship with Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission and one of Sánchez’s main supporters in the European Union, despite their ideological differences, is now of little relevance.

To top it all off, the prime minister came under fire even at Harvard, where he went shortly after his speech at the General Assembly to discuss AI, only to face sharp questions about Spanish politics and corruption. Even his safe role as a statesman was being eroded by political reality. Upon returning from his trip, an attempt to pass legislation that would prevent future situations like Abascal’s (in 2025 alone, there were more than 25,000 evictions, according to data from the General Council of the Judiciary) ran into obstacles in Spain’s fragmented parliament, which rejected every measure, and the legislative session came to a close. Meanwhile, the streets of Madrid and other cities began to fill with tents as people camped out in protest in a country where housing prices are rising by more than 10% annually, well above inflation and more so than wages. Whether it’s a matter of buying (nearly three out of every four Spaniards live in an owner-occupied home) or renting, both the Ministry of Housing and the real estate portal Idealista (which typically lists nearly half a million homes) reported price increases ranging from 30%–40% nationwide, going up to 70% in high-demand areas, during the eight-year period of progressive government, exceeding even the real estate bubble that triggered a 2008 crisis coinciding with the global financial crisis. The country is only just beginning to recover from its impact.

The half-hearted measures approved in previous years to tackle the problem ran into resistance from Spain’s regional governments and city councils controlled by the opposition—the center-right Partido Popular (PP), which governs 13 of Spain’s 19 regions. “Exactly,” the mayor of Madrid, José Luis Martínez-Almeida, said on X in 2021, when opponents accused him of doing “nothing” to tackle the rental crisis in the capital, where the average rent already exceeds the minimum wage.

On October 5, following a tumultuous legislative session in a divided Congress (the more powerful of the two houses in Spain’s parliament), Sánchez announced a snap election. Two days later, Maricarmen Abascal died in the hospital.

If Sánchez loses this election—and even the most optimistic nongovernmental polls, just over a month before the election, give him only between a 5% and 10% chance of winning another term—one of the world’s last bastions of social democracy will disappear along with him. Perhaps the most significant one, both because of the influence Spain has gained within the EU in recent decades and because of the personal leadership Sánchez has exercised in global geopolitics, with the prime minister having spoken out on issues such as climate change; digital governance of AI; the war in Gaza; and, in recent days, European support for Ukraine and migration management. This last issue has even pitted him against another of Europe’s last remaining social democrats (who is also in a precarious coalition), Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen. “Sánchez is the last social democrat who defends a migration policy that is compatible with human rights,” explains political scientist Pablo Simón, a university professor and specialist in electoral systems and political parties, “and he is committed to feminism and environmentalism. Once he leaves office, Spain will be more in line with the majority of Europe and its governments.”

Policies that Sánchez has implemented domestically include granting ministerial status to the 2030 Agenda, elevating the energy transition and the fight against climate change to the level of vice presidency during his terms, and creating the first agencies in any EU country dedicated to AI governance. He has also boasted about these achievements in flawless English—still a novelty among Spanish prime ministers, who have not been particularly fond of languages—at numerous international events. All of this has taken place at a time when the established world order is collapsing, and he has emerged as one of the world leaders who most vocally opposes Donald Trump. When he denied Trump the use of Spanish bases to attack Iran, he directly accused the American president of using “the smoke of war to hide his failure and, in the process, line the pockets of a select few.”

But support for Gaza (not only does Spain recognize Palestine as a state, but Sánchez has also strongly denounced Israel’s actions and labeled them as genocide) and opposition to warmongering leaders like Trump do not win elections on their own. “The debates in Spain are quite similar to those across Europe and focus on the cost of living and immigration, which explain the discontent with governments in many countries,” Simón explains, painting a picture that affects social democrats like Sánchez, leaders further to his right like Macron, and even hard-liners like Giorgia Meloni. The problems of inflation, low wages, loss of purchasing power, and strains on the welfare state are taking their toll on nearly every government in Europe.

Sánchez is, in fact, something of an anomaly with his eight years of resistance—he even titled his book about his political life Manual de Resistencia (Manual of Resistance). Looking ahead to these elections, it appears, on paper, almost impossible for Sánchez to retain his leadership. But if anything has defined his political career, it’s his ability to survive at the last moment, aided by the sociological realities of Spain. Ignacio Urquizu, director of Metroscopia and an election expert, explained a few days ago on SER, Spain’s leading radio network, that it “is the most left-leaning country in Europe, surpassed only by Malta.” He also noted that, since the 1980s, “there has been a straight line” showing that 45% of Spanish society consistently identifies as left-wing or center-left.

Sánchez has always relied on that reality for his historic comebacks. He went from being forced to resign in 2016 as secretary-general of the PSOE (the Spanish socialist party), under pressure from the party apparatus, to regaining that position just two years later and becoming prime minister on the back of a no-confidence motion against corruption, the first of its kind to succeed in Spain. The then future prime minister denounced the corruption that caused “embarrassment, disbelief, and outrage.” He has since survived two elections with the odds stacked against him, without clear majorities, in a Spain that is no longer defined by parties but by blocs, where different forces compete for similar political spaces, leading to parliaments that the framers of Spain’s constitution never anticipated.

The most dramatic of these occurred in 2023, when the right was already uncorking the Champagne, and a single member of parliament tipped the balance in favor of the socialist coalition. It was a poisoned chalice, as Spain has seen: The fact that the PP leader did not become prime minister, due to his failure to reach agreements with several nationalist right parties, paved the way for an ineffective legislative session, with 11 parties and a minority government entangled in parliamentary gridlock and social measures often being blocked by the “no” votes of Sánchez’s supposed allies. This miracle of resilience, in any case, has somehow lasted until now. Even so, Narciso Michavila, president of the social-research firm GAD3, is not ready to declare victory for the right just yet, despite what the polls say: Sánchez, he stated recently, “still has appeal,” and Michavila thinks it is still possible that he will ultimately secure another term.

But there is no denying that in the last decade in Spain, electoral politics have changed. Some of his loyal supporters during the period between 2016 and 2018 are now in prison or awaiting trial for the very corruption that Sánchez denounced. Former minister José Luis Ábalos, once his greatest supporter and whom he even mentioned in the no-confidence-motion speech that eventually led to his becoming prime minister, has now been given a 24-year prison sentence for corruption. Santos Cerdán, the man tasked with reining in the Socialist Party, is awaiting his turn in the dock. The party leadership that came to tackle corruption has proven to be just as, if not more, vulnerable to the recurring cancer of Spanish politics as those they replaced. And although Sánchez boasted about how quickly these incidents were dealt with (there are ministers from the previous administration who are still under investigation for corruption), he has long been unable to boast of integrity as he once did, now that scandals have involved his close associates.

Meanwhile, alongside these proceedings, Sánchez, his party, and many of his allies are denouncing the “judicial persecution” that has extended to the prime minister’s family—his wife, Begoña Gómez, is awaiting trial on various corruption charges, which the prosecutor’s office has opposed on the grounds of insufficient evidence (she has denied the allegations); his brother, David Sánchez, is appealing a nine-year disqualification from holding public office imposed on him by a court in Badajoz for administrative misconduct, stemming from his holding a public position as a cultural manager that was allegedly created specifically for him (he has denied the allegations). Pedro Sánchez has claimed that his brother and wife are “innocent” and victims of a “harassment and bullying operation.”

The latest chapter in this series of trials and investigations surrounding Sánchez was particularly painful for his party and his base: Former Socialist Party president and prime minister of Spain from 2004 to 2011 José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero (who was very active in the last election campaign and served as a role model for Sánchez and his vision of progressivism) was indicted in spring 2026 over an alleged corruption scheme. Jewelry valued at more than a million euros, which Zapatero took months to clarify was supposedly a gift from the Saudi monarchy, was discovered during the searches and sealed his fate. (He has denied any wrongdoing.) The role model Sánchez had looked up to and who boasted of having led the least corrupt government in the history of Spain’s democracy suddenly became the first former prime minister in the country’s democratic history to testify as a defendant. The case is still in the preliminary investigation phase.

But at first, the PSOE came out in force, through press releases and statements from its leaders, to denounce the alleged act of lawfare with the phrase “Whoever can act, should act.” It was a direct quote from the former president of the Partido Popular, José María Aznar, when he attempted to rally opposition to Sánchez’s alliance with Catalan parties in 2023.

These tensions within his family and his party, and the blurring of the lines between the two that the opposition accuses him of, have also spilled over into his campaign. This has put his wife and the developments in her legal case in the spotlight. Sánchez declared he was “deeply in love with” Gómez when he threatened to resign in 2024, following the media harassment of her. “They’ve tried to break us in every way possible, and they’ve achieved exactly the opposite; today we’re more united and stronger than ever,” the prime minister told his wife. “Let them hear it loud and clear: I love you.” The prime minister and his wife’s campaign kisses date back to at least 2016, but this time the Socialist Party has taken up the cause: “We are the party of love,” declared Minister Óscar Puente, and the prime minister has even worn a T-shirt bearing the campaign slogan “La Fuerza del Amor” (“The Power of Love”).

Meanwhile, the far right is poised to become the country’s third-largest political force, now that measures to contain it have failed in Spain, as they have elsewhere in Europe. No measures have succeeded in curbing its rise—or, in cases like Italy, its success at claiming direct power. Spain has, however, long been a country that leans more to the left; it is perhaps the most socially left-leaning country in all of Europe.

“The truth is that the Iberian Peninsula as a whole leans a bit further to the left than its neighbors due to its historical legacy,” says Simón. “In fact, because of this history, socialist parties fare better in Spain and Portugal, and they also do well in the Scandinavian countries.” On the other hand, one need only look at France, where the once all-powerful Socialist Party is now politically irrelevant, to understand the situation in much of the rest of Europe, where centrist parties have lost their influence.

It was the mobilization of Spain’s historic left-leaning majority that saved the PSOE in 2023. This had repercussions in Europe: While other social democratic leaders were falling and the centrists or moderate right-wingers were losing momentum, Sánchez became the voice of a progressive Europe. Emmanuel Macron, who, with Sánchez, built a sort of Spanish-French axis within the European Union, now watches as France burns, six months before an election in which the far right is almost guaranteed to reach at least the runoff round. And all this is unfolding in the midst of what has been described as “Russiagate,” with “foreign interference in all democratic processes in the European Union, including disinformation.”

For Europe, the consequences of this electoral process have already become apparent: The Union had to decide on a far-reaching budget, which also includes the future of Ukraine—whose president has warned that the country needs an additional 70 billion euros that Europe does not currently have. This is especially true following the revelation by Poland’s foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, that the EU has been left on its own in its contribution to Ukraine’s defense and rearmament: “Since January of last year, the United States has not contributed a single cent to Ukraine’s defense. We, Europe, are doing it.” But the elections in Spain are the start of a chain of electoral contests—France and Italy will follow—that push the possibility of an agreement further out of reach. European negotiations often drag on for years, and any electoral upheaval can derail those already underway. One of Sánchez’s most loyal ministers, Luis Planas, for example, will not appear on any electoral lists so he can devote all his time in office to these negotiations: “Between now and the end of the year, the future of the common agricultural policy and the fisheries policy is at stake,” which in Spain accounts for nearly 9% of GDP through both direct and indirect contributions.

The elections will be held on November 29 amid a tense atmosphere: The right is resorting to personal attacks and AI-generated deepfakes against Sánchez, his wife, and his cabinet. Left-wing forces have not found a figurehead like Jean-Luc Mélenchon of the France Insoumise (France Unbowed) party and are polling at less than 10%—a situation that would leave the PSOE without strong coalition partners even if it performs well. Sánchez’s international standing and the strength of the macroeconomy will likely have little weight in an election where the focus is on basic issues including the cost of living and specifically housing. But whatever the outcome, it will likely be the first in a series of elections that may lay bare the crisis facing liberal democracies in Europe. Now without the protection of the United States, it faces two existential crises. There’s an internal crisis, marked by the rise of the far right and its contempt for human rights, and an external crisis, with the Russian threat becoming clearer by the day and commercial and technological pressure from the United States and China, which has counted Sánchez among its most important advocates in its dealings with Europe.

#3649. Phantom Blade Zero Put Up Some Massive Sales Numbers

Developer S-Game's action-RPG Phantom Blade Zero launched on October 29 and had a massive start across PC and PS5.

The game sold more than 4 million copies over its first 72 hours. That works out to 926 units sold per minute or about 15.4 per second over the first three days.

"Thank you everyone from the bottom of our hearts for all the love and support," the studio said in a social media post.

The 4 million figure counts copies sold across both PC and PS5--the game is not available on Xbox. The game reached a record of 833,921 peak concurrent users on Steam on November 1.

The game's developer is based in China, and the majority of preorders for the game came from China, Taiwan, and Hong Kong.

Phantom Blade Zero's sales out of the gate are strong, but do not come close to another hit game from the Chinese game developer scene, Black Myth: Wukong. That game sold 10 million copies over its first three days. The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom, meanwhile, sold 10 million copies in three days as well.

If you’re looking to get started, you can check out our Phantom Blade Zero guides hub for many walkthroughs on increasing your power and finding rare items.

“S-Game’s Wuxia-inspired combat puts you in the middle of a Chinese action movie,” Richard Wakeling wrote in GameSpot’s Phantom Blade Zero review.

#3648. Lions Coach Dan Campbell Shares Update on Linebacker Jack Campbell's Injury

Detroit Lions head coach Dan Campbell is providing a hopeful update on linebacker Jack Campbell’s hospitalization after his on-field injury.

“It’s not easy because he’s gonna always be on our minds over here,” Dan, 50, said during an appearance on “Costa and Jansen with Heather” on Detroit’s 97.1 The Ticket on Tuesday, November 3, per The Athletic. “The good news is he is improving, but we also — we got a job to do, and this is what we’re tasked with, and there’s a reason why we go through all this stuff.

He continued, “It’s to get to where we wanna go collectively as a team, and adversity comes in all shapes and sizes and we gotta overcome everything that comes our way.”

Jack, 26, appeared motionless after a tackle against Minnesota Vikings tight end T.J. Hockenson during the Sunday, November 1, game at Detroit’s Ford Field. He was then transported off the field, where wife Megan Campbell was seen meeting him. Jack was subsequently taken to a local hospital.

The team provided an update on Jack’s condition on Monday, November 2, sharing that the linebacker “continues to rest and recover” at the hospital and that “preliminary indications are positive.” The Lions, however, declined to share further information at the time “out of respect for Jack and his family.”

Dan, for his part, has been communicative with the team’s captains about Jack’s health and they have conveyed the latest updates with the rest of the Lions crew.

“I think the thought of him — knowing he’s doing better — I’ve kept the captains up to date and they’ve let the other guys know it’s good news,” Dan, who is not related to Jack despite their shared last name, said on Tuesday. “So, I think that helps everybody just get a better handle on all this. Once you know that, then you gotta move on for yourself, too, in that moment because if you let things wander and you drift and you worry a little and then you’re trying to play or prepare, that’s where bad things can happen to you because you’re not all in on what you need to be doing.”

Dan continued, “So, that’s why it’s important that you get back to your own business. All we can do at this point is just continue to pray for Jack, put our thoughts on him when we have a minute, and his family, and it’s working, like I said, because he is improving.”

#3647. When Is Resident Evil Coming To Home Video? It Could Be Very Soon

Zach Cregger's Resident Evil movie crushed it at the box office, banking more than $400 million globally to become the most successful entry in the series ever. When will the film be available to watch at home, though?

According to Fandango, the home video release is set for November 3. That's apparently when people can buy the movie outright or rent it digitally, with a physical edition for Blu-ray coming at some point later. It will also presumably come to streaming at some point, and it should hit Netflix given the multi-billion-dollar Pay-1 deal the two companies have in place.

While we wait, Netflix just announced that director Paul W.S. Anderson's original Resident Evil, along with its follow-up, Resident Evil: Apocalypse, are now available to stream.

They join the other Resident Evil movies already on Netflix, including Resident Evil: Afterlife, Resident Evil: Retribution, Resident Evil: Extinction, and Resident Evil: The Final Chapter. The 2022 Resident Evil TV show is also currently streaming on Netflix.

While the new Resident Evil movie may be coming to home video on November 3, it's also staying in theaters. In fact, it was just announced that the movie is returning to IMAX and other premium large format (PLF) screens.

Cregger, who co-wrote and directed the new Resident Evil movie, recently discussed the backlash from the hardcore gamer community. He said he should have known better that fans of the games wouldn't embrace him and his ideas. After the movie came out and got great reviews and made tons of money, Cregger said he felt "gratified."

The filmmaker has said he has ideas for more Resident Evil movies, but he's not going to pursue them; instead, he's only going to make original, non-franchise movies going forward. His next movie, The Flood, is a sci-fi film starring Jennifer Lawrence.

#3646. Former Xbox Exec Shares Her Side Of The Story After Mysterious Depature

Helen Chiang, the veteran Xbox staffer who got promoted in July and left the company amid mysterious circumstances just recently, has shared her side of the story--but her response doesn't close the book on this saga.

In a LinkedIn post titled "Clarity is Kindess," which itself is a reference to her former boss (and Xbox CEO) Asha Sharma's much-ridiculed and cringey mantra, said it's "not accurate" that she was "fired for a policy violation" as multiple reports said.

Chiang said she will not "turn this into a play-by-play" and reveal the specifics, but she wanted to speak out to dispel rumors. "What has been said about my departure, and what has been left unsaid, has created a picture of me that I hardly recognize."

She went on to "set the record straight" by claiming she did not leak confidential company information to the press as some had speculated. "I have never communicated with any journalist outside the limited, company-authorized interviews I’ve done as part of my job," she said, adding that this includes having no contact with any journalist who reached out to her before today to ask for her side of the story.

Chiang went on to say she did not leave Xbox to join a competitor. "You don’t spend two decades somewhere without developing a deep loyalty to the people, teams, and businesses you’ve helped build," she said

"Xbox was never just another stop in my career. My end game was always to keep building here," she said.  

That may all be true, but it's also unquestionable that people regularly spend lengthy periods of their career at one company, in high-level positions, and then move to other companies.

Third, Chiang said she "did not engage in discrimination, bullying, harassment, insider trading, embezzlement, or other fraudulent activity."

"I stand by my record: both the results I delivered and the way I have treated people throughout my career. I won’t let speculation define my character or erase that record," she said.

Chiang added that she did not leave Xbox because she was "passed over for a bigger role." She said that since having children, she became more "intentional about how I define ambition and success." She said she has purposefully not sought out bigger roles or jobs with more responsibilities; she said she hadn't interviewed for a job since 2011.

"My reputation and results paved the way for the opportunities that followed. I went where the company believed I was needed and where I could have the greatest impact," she said, adding that she did not ask to become Xbox's first-ever COO.

"I believe in fairness, accountability, and holding ourselves to the standards we expect of others. Those standards only mean something when they’re applied consistently," she said.

Chiang said she has "serious concerns" about how those standards were applied in her case, and she said those concerns "deserve to be taken seriously."

"I share this because I don’t want my departure reduced to an inaccurate story about incompetence, ambition for the next big job, or a Nelson-level scandal. My story is about staying true to your core values, especially when it is hard," she said. "That’s the legacy I hope to leave behind."

Chiang's statement doesn't spell out the specific nature surrounding her departure from Xbox, so many will naturally want more answers. Those could come in time, as Chiang said this is "not the whole story."

Another former Xbox executive, Shannon Loftis, commented on Chiang's post to say she is "Team Helen all the way." Loftis said she wonders who may have leaked the "false information" about Chiang and what their motivations may have been. In any event, she says it shows a "loss of moral character and 'clarity' in leadership at Xbox."

"A real leadership team would have relentlessly pursued the 'leaker' and taken appropriate action because 'confidential personnel matters' actually are bases for defamation lawsuits," she said. "It's a clownshow up in there and I feel terrible for anyone that still has to deal with it."

A spokesperson for Microsoft told Windows Central that the company does not “discuss individual personnel matters.”

According to a source speaking to Eurogamer, Chiang was “terminated for policy violations.” The Verge’s Tom Warren backed this up, saying Chiang was cut loose due to a “policy violation,” but the exact nature of that is unknown.

In July, Sharma announced that Chiang would become Xbox’s first-ever COO, with “end-to-end” responsibility for the financial future of Xbox’s content, hardware, platform, and services.

Chiang had worked at Microsoft for 20 years, in that time playing a key role in the creation of Xbox Live and later shepherding Mojang and the lucrative Minecraft franchise. As COO, Chiang was expected to “bring our businesses together under one operating model, making sure we make clear investment decisions, learn from our successes and failures, and hold ourselves accountable for results,” Sharma said.

For her part, Sharma said she will have an update to share on the COO position at Xbox at some point, but she didn’t divulge more.

The Xbox business was “not healthy” when Sharma took over, she said, and Chiang no doubt had a challenging road ahead of her. As for now, however, people can only speculate as to the real reason she left Xbox.
